translations.text: Discourse of our holy and blessed father Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, on the making of man,
which he wrote to his brother Peter, bishop of Sebaste.

If the glory of those who have acquired virtue had to be measured by the value of possessions, all the boasts of wealth would be found worthless when we compared them with your virtues, according to the saying of Solomon the wise,
for the grace that is worthy of you is above the value of riches.
And now the feast has summoned us.

Of the holy and glorious Fulfilment, according to the former custom, to the mercy [?] your friendship [?], and we offer to your greatness, O man of God, a small gift, such as is worthy of you, yet not less than our ability.
And this gift is a discourse, like a shabby garment woven with labor by a poor mind.

As for the occasion of this discourse, I think that many will suppose that this undertaking of ours came about through presumption, an undertaking of which we were neither worthy nor under obligation.

Yet holy Basil, the father and teacher of all, is not far from the obligation of justice: he alone investigates among the creatures of God the one rightly created, truly in the likeness of God, whose soul is as an image of its Creator.

He made known the commandment [?] of the hidden creatures of God and made them manifest and intelligible to those who sought it. But we fall short with regard to his wonders, which are laid upon us [?] from his glories and awesome things. And it seemed right to us, out of the obligation of justice, to complete what remained of that earlier exposition of the wise teacher concerning the creation of man.
It is not that we regard this discourse of his, in which we have taken part through this discourse of ours, as deficient.
May this not be so concerning that glorious mouth, as though it had been made contemptible or deficient by this discourse of ours.
But so that no one may suppose that the glory of the teacher is diminished among his disciples,

and if his discourse on the creation of the six days had in truth been deficient, and none of his disciples had striven to complete what remained of it, left unexplained by him, there would be a pretext and cause against the teacher, since he had not produced among his disciples the ability to understand and to expound.
Therefore let us boldly take it upon ourselves to complete what was left over from that earlier work.
And if anything is found in this discourse of ours that deserves to be said to come from his teaching, then it is a confirmation for him.

And if this discourse of ours is [?] to his subtle reasonings, then he is blameless, since no ability to attain to them was found among his disciples. Let us be the blameworthy ones and confess our deficiency to our accusers, since our heart did not contain that wisdom of the teacher. And it seemed right to me that what we have prepared in this discourse of ours is not inferior to the wonders that are among creatures, but above and higher than all those things that can be understood,
for nothing among beings is like God,
…like the making of man. For this reason we will be forgiven more readily by those who have attained holiness than by those who do not listen.

And our discourse may be found to fall short of what is fitting and of what is required of us. We must examine what came first and has passed, what exists now, and what is yet to be, so that nothing among existing things remains unexamined. We have [?] undertaken to search out and recount matters established among men. But some things are thought to lie outside this account of the Scriptures concerning which man was created [?], and these do not now appear in it. We will make these clear from the Scriptures and from what we draw out of the treasury of the mind. In this way our discourse may be held together on every side by the help of divine power. That power gives the strength to understand and the hope of reaching what cannot be reached, and it leads the way where there is no other means.

I thought it right to set out a division of these discourses of ours into headings, so that the meaning of each part set down may be known quickly. 1: Chapter 1: On the nature of the earth as one part, and a detailed account of the things created before man. 2: Chapter 2: Why man was created last of all created things. 3: Chapter 3: That the nature of man is more honourable than all the created things that have appeared. 4: Chapter 4: That the make of man signifies rule and authority in every respect. 5: Chapter 5: That man is like the kingship of the Godhead. 6:

Chapter 6: An examination of those who mix the mind with nature, which includes a refutation of the statements of the heretics. 7: Chapter 7: Why man was created bare of his own weapons and of natural clothing. 8: Chapter 8: Why the form of man stands upright, and that hands were created for the sake of reason, and an examination of the divisions of souls. 9: Chapter 9: That the body of man was created as an instrument for reason. 10: Chapter 10: That the mind does its work through the senses. 11: Chapter 11: That the nature of the mind is invisible. 12: Chapter 12: An examination of the treasury of the mind, and a natural account of laughter and weeping. 13: Chapter 13: On sleep, yawning, and dreams.

14: Chapter 14: That the mind does not reside in one part of the body, and a distinction between spiritual and bodily movements. 15: Chapter 15: On the soul: that the rational soul is truly and properly called soul, while the others are called soul only by sharing the name; and that the whole power of the mind is spread through the entire body, in each member according to its capacity. 16: Chapter 16: An examination of what God said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." And in it is the inquiry concerning the likeness: how the passible resembles the one who has no passion, and the mortal the immortal, and how male and female can exist among those who are like God. 17: Chapter 17: What shall we reply to those who ask about procreation and fertility, if it came about after sin, and, if man had not sinned, where the souls would have come from? 18: Chapter 18: That the animal impulse established in us is there because of our kinship with them.

19. Chapter 19: Concerning those who say that the good delights to come will consist of food and drink, because in the beginning man was commanded to live by these two. 20. Chapter 20: What is the life that is in Paradise, and what is the tree from which they were kept back? 21. Chapter 21: That the assurance of the resurrection is to be expected through the multiplication of forms, one after another, more than from what is said in the Scriptures. 22. Chapter 22: Concerning those who ask: If the resurrection is good and sweet, why has it not happened already, instead of our awaiting it after many ages? 23. Chapter 23: Concerning those who acknowledge the beginning of the world, even if unwillingly, that it is fitting for them to acknowledge its end as well. 24. Chapter 24: A reply to those who say that:

matter is without beginning alongside God. 25. Chapter 25: How those who deny the faith may accept what the Scriptures say concerning the resurrection. 26. Chapter 26: That the resurrection is not a matter of necessity [?]. 27. Chapter 27: That it is possible for human bodies to exist again from the four elements of the earth after their dissolution, and for those of one kind to be separated out, each as its own portion from among all things. 28. Chapter 28: Concerning those who say that souls were created before bodies, or bodies before souls. The refutation of the argument of those who maintain that souls dwell in many bodies. 29. Chapter 29: An inquiry showing that the being of the soul and of the body is united. 30. Chapter 30: An account drawn from physicians, showing the members of human bodies in their formation; and it is a brief account.
Chapter 1. He spoke in the first chapter about the nature of the earth in a single part, and gave a detailed disclosure. Concerning the things created before man, Scripture said:
"This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth,"
for all visible things were completed, and each existing thing went off to its own place and was set apart, and then
the body of heaven encompassed everything, and those heavy and dense bodies, that is, earth and water, were made fast against one another in the middle of the world.
And their firmness and strength was the wisdom of the Godhead and the power within the nature of all things, for the governing of all things.

And by motion and rest this was contrived: the bringing into being of things not yet created, and the continuance of created things, which were made from that dense nature that does not move, but is a cart's wheel,
that is, the swift motion of heaven, sending it around in a circle and preserving them together, strengthened by the power of firmness, around which it turns with swift motion, and that is the earth.
But the firmament of heaven, which does not stop and does not come to rest by standing still, which does not move so as ever to fall [?].
And the motion of the falling [?] above and the awe of the working of these visible things are equal. I mean their nature and their striking [?].
And that motion which does not stop; but the earth does not move from its firmness, and heaven does not rest from its motion.
And these were created in the beginning by the wisdom of their Creator, and he distributed all the natures that change and are transformed.

And this, as I suppose, was the ordered arrangement of the statement that Moses the prophet made: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," for all the visible and perceptible things among created beings exist in motion and in rest.
But when heaven and earth were made, they were not of one operation, but opposed to each other;
and the many created things between them were joined, compounded and fastened to one another, and by this the extremes of visible things, that is, heaven and earth, were joined together.
For air resembles the subtlety of fire, which is always in motion, since the nature of air is subtle;
it is like that motion of fire and does not descend heavily, but stands as a boundary and divider among those visible things.
And in the same way the moist nature, that is, water, was made joined to those two opposing natures.

Because of their heaviness and density, I liken them closely to the nature of earth. Because of their moisture and flowing, I liken them to the moving nature of air. So you find the two natures, though far apart, joined together through what lies between them. But the true account, once grasped, is this:
the nature of opposites is truly mixed together with one another,
so that all created things may follow one upon another and each created thing may be joined to its own nature, even though their individual properties are opposed.
For motion is not recognized only by a swift change of place, but it also occurs as turning and alteration; and again the unmoving [?], when it does not admit the motion of turning.
The wisdom of God exchanged the properties of the two, so that what moves became unchanging and what is unmoving became changeable.
And God determined this for this reason: so that the property of divinity, which is far from alteration and turning, should not be found in any created thing,
and so that a created thing should not be supposed to be the Creator, for what turns and alters is not God.
And therefore the earth is unmoving yet undergoes change, while heaven neither changes nor is unmoving.

And for this reason the power of divinity exchanged the properties of the two, making the unmoving changeable and the moving unchangeable, in order to join them to each other and to remove from them any supposition of divinity,
for God is outside these two conditions, alteration and immobility.
And at that time everything came to be in its fullness and its measure, as the Book has said, for it says: "The heaven and the earth were finished."
And all things were adorned with their own beauty: heaven with the brilliance of the luminaries,
the sea and the air with the living creatures that move about in them,

and the earth was filled with plants, with shoots of many colours, and with everything that springs from the earth, which at once grew strong by the will of God. And the earth became full of beautiful flowers, which bloomed before the fruit.
And when they sprang up from the earth, they flourished and hastened toward maturity.

And all creation is joyful by the command of God, when every shoot and plant flourishes, and all the creatures that graze in their many colors, those that hasten to the cliffs and crevices, and all the birds that call and wheel [?], which hasten to the groves and [?].
And again, the sight of the sea,

when it happens to be calm and at rest after its agitation, gathered into its own bed, surrounded and walled in by the sands by the command of God; and again the gentle movement of those salty waves, which resembles the beauty of all things that are swayed by that pleasant and harmless breeze, and it folds gently upon the back of the water.
And all the riches of creation had been made ready on the dry lands and the seas, but their ruler had not yet appeared.

Chapter 2. And he spoke on the second chapter: Why was man created last of all creatures? This creature, great and honored, I mean man, was not yet found among the beauty of existing things, for it was not fitting that the ruler should appear before his realm.
Rather, it was truly fitting that the kingdom be prepared first, and only then that the king should appear.

And when the Creator of all had prepared the royal treasury, which is this earth, the sea and the confluences, and this sky, which is a covering [?] over them, he stored up all wealth in this treasury,
that is, the wealth of all creatures, of plants and shoots and animals, and all those that have soul and breath.

And if you wish to count up the wealth of natures, and which of them are beautiful in the eyes of men: the likeness of gold and silver, and these precious, shining stones, which seemed wonderful to men,

For all these things were stored up for man in the bosom of the earth, like the treasuries of kings. And after this He brought him forth into the world, so that he might behold the wonders that are in them and be lord over those good things, and so that he might understand that gift of His,
in which he might delight, and might know the power of his Creator, which is ineffable, from those visible things and from the beauties of creatures and their magnificent things.
And for this reason he brought man into the world last of the creatures, not that he placed him last because he held him in contempt,

but so that he might be king from his very creation, just as when someone wishes to hold a supper, it is fitting for him first to prepare what is needed for food, and only then to summon the distinguished guests.
And again, he should adorn his house and table fittingly, and only then bring in the guests to eat his bread.
And in just this way did the Nourisher of our nature, the rich one and King, act: when he had adorned creation with every beauty and prepared this great and honored dwelling,
only then did he bring man in and give him as his task a choice possession, found and made ready.
And for this reason he placed in him a twofold ground of life and mixed the divine with the earthly, so that he might be called and bear the name of both:
the one of God, by the nature of the mind, and the other from the good things of the earth, for enjoyment through bodily perception.
Chapter 3. And he spoke concerning the third chapter, that the nature of man is more honorable than all that appear among created things. It is fitting

that we not leave this too uninvestigated: for the creation of this glorious earth from these four elements took place swiftly, and it came into being by the power of God and was raised up immediately by the command of God.
But deliberation precedes the making of man:

how what is made should be shaped, and what form it should have from the Creator, and how it is fitting for it to be, and to what he should liken it, and what it should become, and what its work should be, and when it should be created, and over what it should rule.
The form came first in all of this, so that his rule came to be before his creation, and before he existed he acquired rule, as the book said:
"And God said: 'Let us make man in our image and likeness.
And let him rule over the fish of the sea and the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky and the cattle and all the earth.'"
O wonder! For when the sun was being created, no deliberation preceded it, nor did any precede that of the earth and the sky.

And all those that were created by his word were created with no depiction of whence or how. And likewise all beings, among which are air and mist and stars, sea and earth and animals and plants, all these were made by the word of God. But the making of man alone the Creator of all carried out with careful establishing, to the point that he prepared material for him for his establishing. And he likened him to that beautiful root, and set out beforehand in brief
what was made for him, in order to create a nature likened to the work for which he was created.

Chapter 4. And he spoke concerning the fourth chapter, that: The way man is constructed signifies a ruling, sovereign power in every respect. And just as craftsmen make a vessel suited to its use and shape it with skill, so too the Maker of our nature, the wise Creator, created him as a royal vessel, with virtues of the soul and adornments of the body, so that he would be fit to be a royal vessel.

And the soul signifies by its name its own loftiness, when it is removed from subjection and made independent by its own deliberation, and is not under compulsion but proceeds by its own will in its own governance.

And these virtues belong to none other than an honored king. And in this it is like the nature that is master of all. And this signifies that it is a royal nature. And just as painters depict the likenesses of kings in their form and adornment, and call that image a king, so too is the nature of man, for he made it ruler over those other living creatures, in the likeness of the King of all.
It was given the name king not because the adornment of kings clothed it,
a crown or some other such thing, so that its kingship would be signified by that, but because virtue clothed it,

which signifies that true kingship more than any garments, adorned with the crown of righteousness, which is all the more fitting, that it be related [?] in beauty to that root to which it was likened.
Chapter 5. And he spoke concerning the fifth chapter, that:
Man is like the kingship of the Godhead. But divine beauty is not depicted by the beauty of colours but by a higher order, which cannot be expressed or grasped by the understanding.
And just as painters work with many colours made from various pigments, and mix them all as is fitting, so that they may make the likeness match the beauty of the original exactly,

so too understand the Creator's work: He adorned human nature with many virtues, like beautiful colours, and in proportion to His own power displayed in us an adornment made of everything by which that true life is known,
not with bright reds or any other pigment that painters mix in for the beauty of the image, nor with black,
with which they draw the eyebrows and eyes, along with the other colours, to adorn the image,
as painters skilfully do. Instead of these, He used purity, holiness, simplicity and separation from all evil.
And by such a form man resembles his Creator, and with this color the Creator adorned his image, that is, our nature.
And if you turn your mind to look at those other qualities by which the beauty of God is known, then you will find the likeness in our nature.
The Godhead is mind and word, for "In the beginning was the Word." And those who are counted with Paul the apostle "have the mind of Christ," which speaks in them.
And man is not far from these, for word and wisdom are seen in you, in the likeness of that true Word. And mind.
And further, it is said again that God is love and the source of love, as John the Evangelist said: "Love is from God, and God is love." And the Creator of nature made this the mark for us and said:
"By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another." And when this feature is not found, the likeness has been changed in turn.
And since God sees all things, hears all this and searches out all things, you too have good sight and hearing, and a living wisdom by which you search out all things.
Chapter 6. And he spoke concerning the sixth chapter, an inquiry

into the things that join the mind with nature, and in it the refutation of what the heretics have said. And let no one suppose that I am saying that God receives knowledge of existing things through many powers; for it cannot be said, in an account of God, that there are many active powers.
Nor again is there in us a power that is many and of various forms by which we perceive anything, even though we apprehend through many senses.
But the power is one: I mean the mind implanted in us, which operates in all things through the senses.
Although nature has many senses,
yet the one that makes them act and governs them is one, even with the multitude of things that come to be, and the nature does not change.
Now then, just as someone becomes senseless and says that God is divided on account of his many works, that by a manifold power he is the creator of the eyes,

As the prophet said, "and he who planted the ears." And this was said according to the custom of human natures, concerning that knowing power; and he said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness."

And we say: Where are those heretics who deny the likeness? What, then, do they say to this utterance, and how will their defense be justified, concerning which it was said and they say: How then can one image be a likeness of divided persons?
And if the Son is not like the Father, how then does he make the image of [?] for divided natures?
For he who said, "Let us make in our image," spoke with the plural of the Trinity, and did not mention the image in the singular only.

If the originals do not resemble one another, their image cannot be one. And if the natures are separate, the images must be separate too, and He would create for each nature an image resembling each one.
But when the image is one and the original is not one, and that which is foolish and cut off from its own mind becomes senseless [?],
how could it resemble the one, since they are like one another [?]?
And was this saying not perhaps spoken for the dispelling of this evil, for the sake of human life, namely:
"Let us make man in our image and likeness"?

Chapter 7. And he spoke, concerning the seventh chapter, of why man was created naked of his weapons and of natural clothing; what, then, does the formation of man with upright stance signify, and how is it that no natural animal strength came to be in us?

But he brought man into this world empty of natural weapons, unclothed, and what is more, poor and lacking all the things needful for his life. And truly he seems more to be pitied than to be praised, for he is not armed with a growth of horns, nor of claws, nor of hooves and shanks, nor of [?].
And there is nothing at all in his nature with which he could ward off what harms him, as many animals have means against encounters with what harms them.

And his body is not covered with a garment of hair either. It was fitting that the ruler be fortified and armed within his own nature, so that he would not need anything external to protect and cover his flesh. And now, behold, we see the lion and the boar,
the leopard and the tiger, and other animals as well, which have within their own nature what they need to protect themselves by their own strength,

which is in them: as the bull has horns, and the hare swiftness, and the gazelle leaping and brightness of eyes, and others again bulk of body, and birds wings, and the bee a sting. And with all of them something needful is found, even if only one thing, for their own protection.

But man alone among all these is deficient, for in swiftness he is slow, and he is smaller in body among those great of body, and more [?] among those that are armed. Now then, in what way can he be king over all the animals?
But it is not difficult for us to show that what is thought by them to be a need of his nature is the very cause of his rule.
And if it had been in the nature of man to be swifter than the horse, and moreover that his feet should not be worn down [?] because of their hardness,
which consists in the firmness of hooves and legs, or if he had horns and sharp claws and a sting like a bee's, he would truly be an ugly beast to look at, if he had all these things in his body.
And again, he would be heedless of ruling over those he rules, if he had no need of them.

For this reason the things he needs were distributed among all those subjected to him, so that his rule over them might be a matter of necessity, just as all the kings of the earth receive what they need from those over whom they rule.
And because of our slowness and heaviness we needed the horse, and we subjected it to ourselves,

and because of the nakedness of our flesh we needed to acquire sheep, so that the lack in our nature regarding clothing might be made good. And for this reason we take wool year by year, and other necessary things as well,
which we need of necessity for the means of our life, and these compel us to acquire those beasts of burden,
and since we cannot graze like cattle, we acquired oxen to be subject to us, so that the means of our life might be made easy by their labor.

And further, we also needed teeth for biting, so that with them we might drive off those among the many animals that fight against us. For this reason the dog with its speed suffices us, like a sword in a man's hand.
And again, iron is for man sharper and harder than horns and sharp claws.

And these are not implanted in our flesh, as the weapons of beasts are implanted in their bodies, but are to be taken up at the proper time, to help us in time of need, and then to be laid back in their place.

And again, as for the turnings [?] of the crocodile, it is fitting that we cover ourselves with its own hide, and if that cannot be found at the time of need, that we obtain something like it made of iron, with which we may be protected in time of trouble and then be freed of that burden in time of peace.
And again, the wing of birds came to serve men, since we cannot catch birds by speed.
and some of them are brought under control for the use of hunters,
and by certain means they serve our needs. We use feathers for arrows, and because of the bow the bird does not escape us.
And so that the feet might be able to manage the length of a journey without being hurt, we obtained footwear from animals for our use.

Chapter 8. And he spoke in the eighth chapter about why the form of man is upright, and that the hands were created for the sake of reason, and an inquiry into the divisions of the soul. The stature of man is upright and raised toward heaven, and he beholds that which is above all these things; appointed as king, it signifies in every way the ways of rule.
And this signification is true, for all the subject creatures look down, toward the ground, but man alone stands with his head raised. The other animals are bowed in body,
signifying their subjection to rule, for the front parts of all of them are feet and not hands. And therefore, being bowed, they need a support.
But man's forelimbs are hands. Because his stature is upright, he does not need supports, only the two feet set apart for standing. Moreover, the hands are helpers for reason.
And if someone were to say that the special purpose of the hands among human beings is to serve speech, he would not be mistaken.

And not only for this fitting purpose, that we answer one another in writing, through the dexterity of the hands, in the service of speech, although this too is not far removed from the gift of speech,
for by writing we converse and speak by means of the hands, and the letters of writing [?] answer like speaking voices.
But let me consider something else as well and say that the hands are helpers in the uttering of speech.
And before the examination of that matter, let us turn diligently to the discourse, so that what we must say on this occasion may not slip past us.
Now why were plants created before animals, and then animals, and then human beings? Not only for this reason,
that animals are nourished by plants and human beings by animals; rather, this is what I think:

that by this the prophet Moses indicated a hidden teaching of mystery and explained a subtle inquiry concerning souls, which those outside philosophers conjectured about, yet they did not perceive in it the true disclosure.
But I think that this passage signifies that souls are divided into three kinds.
I mean the power of growth, the power of sensation, and the soul itself, of which one is the growing plant.
And in it is found the power of life without sensation.

The second of these is the growing kind, as we mentioned, in which there is the governance of sense perception. It is found among the irrational animals. It does not only grow and flourish; its activity also comes from the senses. But perfect life is found in the nature of man, that is, the rational life,
which grows, perceives and reasons.
And its governance is through the mind.
For this reason we divided beings in this way: some of them are intellectual and some are bodily.
The intellectual is not to be examined now, and as for the bodily, some of it is entirely without life, and some of it has life.
Among the bodies of living things, some are alive with sense perception and some have no sense perception.

Among the beings that have sense perception, some are rational and some are irrational. For this reason plants also came into being before the other beings, after the lifeless elements, that is, earth and water, air and fire.
And in these plants is found a soul without sensation.

These were created first, and after them were created the sentient, irrational animals, without understanding, for this reason: that the mind does not dwell in a body unless it is blended with a sentient body.
And therefore man was created after the plants and the animals, and in him he made the way of nature everlasting,
for man is blended from all those various souls. And he is nourished by the power of the vegetative soul that is in him.

And together with this he received the sensitive soul, which is between sensation and plants, coarser than the rational soul and finer than the vegetative soul. Then came about the blending of the subtle nature, which shines with that intellectual torch. Because of this the constitution of man came to be from these three, as we have learned from the apostle Paul,
This is what he writes to the Ephesians, and he prays to God for them, that he may grant that perfect grace to the body, the soul and the spirit at the resurrection of Christ.
By mentioning the body he wished to indicate the vegetative nature; [?] by mentioning the soul, to indicate the sensitive nature; and by mentioning the spirit, to indicate the rational nature.
And for this reason it was said to the man learned in the law, in the Gospel, that he should love God with all his heart and with all his strength and with all his understanding.

And this again, as I think, points to this division. When he mentioned the heart, he wished to show us the body; by mentioning strength, he wished to show us the soul; and by mentioning understanding, he wished to show us the mind. The Apostle also teaches that the disposition is divided into three kinds. The first of them is carnal, occupied with what goes down into the belly and with its pleasures;
the second is psychical (soulish), which moves between good and evil,
and this is higher than the first, yet it has not attained the measure of holiness;

but the third is spiritual, and in it is the perfection of its excellence. For this reason he reproaches the Corinthians for their deficiency and says, "You are still carnal," and you do not receive perfect teaching.

And again he says, when he distinguishes the middle and the perfect: "But the soulish man does not accept what is from the Spirit, for it seems foolishness to him. But the spiritual man judges all things, and he is judged by no one."
And just as the soulish is superior to the carnal, so likewise the spiritual is superior to the soulish.

And when Scripture said above that man was created after all the soul-endowed creatures, it indicated that the rational spirit is among the other souls, and that those two are found within it, that is, the soulish and the vegetative.
And since man is a rational living being, it was therefore fitting that his hands too should be made suited to speech,

just as we see with practitioners of an art [?] and with [?], each of whom prepares an instrument suited to his own art [?]: one cannot pipe on the lyre, nor play the lyre on the pipe, because of the difference between their instruments.
In the same way it was fitting for the human instruments to be made suited to speech and conversation, so that discourse might be displayed through the instrument of the voice.

And for this reason hands were created for the body. The works of the hands in their use are countless. With skill and design they take up and put down whatever their work requires in every craft, in the struggle of battle and in time of peace, on sea and on land.

But before all these things, hands were created in human nature for the sake of speech. If man had lacked hands, he would have been like the four-footed beasts in taking food, in all their diverse kinds and the varied forms in which they were created. And if man had no hands, how could his voice be formed into articulate speech, when his mouth would be occupied as the mouths of beasts are?
But now, since hands have been given to the body, the mouth has been made free for discourse and conversation.
And the hands are the property of man, for the Creator created them in man for the furtherance of speech.

Chapter 9. And it says concerning the ninth chapter that the human body was created as an instrument for speech. For our Creator gave us that divine grace in our nature when he made in his likeness the special character of the good things that are his,
But we say that he gave us wisdom and understanding, and in his goodness granted us his own likeness and the beauty of his own beauty.
For the mind is intelligible and bodily [?], and the movement of its grace could not be shown except by some means. For this reason its body was created in this form,
so that it would have a voice, and the way its creation was arranged points to the form of its movement. And just as a skilled musician wishes, in his own music,
to make his skill known, and to show it in his own voice.

And when he cannot do this with the strength of his own voice, he shows his skill through other voices, through instruments that he sounds when he makes music. From lifeless things he brings out a blended sound, from the pipe or the lyre and similar instruments. In the same way the human mind cannot show its activity in its various forms except through the senses.
And for this reason it was summoned [?], so that this instrument might be vocal, and by it might show hidden thought and reveal inner matters.
And this kind of music was made in man as a blend of lyre and pipe, as if they were sounding together. It works like this:
the air comes out from its place and passes through a person's windpipe when he wishes to speak and wants his voice to come out.
Then by that inner movement it makes to resound [?] that pipe, which is the throat, likened to the [?] of the flute.
And this is like a flute producing sound from the cords by which it is encircled.
And the throat draws what comes out of the [?] into that pipe, from the two passages that are in the organ of smell at the palate, and thereby it divides the sound, and the sound becomes audible.
And the cheeks, the tongue, and the structure that moves the jaw by loosening and tightening,
by stretching and drawing together, are all like the movement of the powers [?] of the lyre as it sounds, and at the moment when it wants to blend the sound quickly.
And the opening of the lips and their closing are like the movement of the fingers on the holes of the flute in bringing forth the sound.

In this way the mind, by means of that instrument, produced speech in us, and we were found to be speaking. And the grace of speech could not have been found in us if our eating were by the labor of the lips, like the beasts, who bend down to eat with them.
Now since this service has been transferred to the hand of man, the mouth became free, set apart for the utterance of words.
And the operation in this instrument is twofold: the one for the production of sound, and the other for the reception of hearing that comes from outside.
And these are not mixed with each other, but each remains at the work commanded by nature, neither of them harming its fellow.

For the voice does not hear, nor does hearing speak. Rather, the one, which is the mouth, is always sending out and giving forth, and the other, which is the ear, is always receiving and taking in without wearying, as Solomon the wise said; and this is very marvelous:
What then is the extent of that place into which all of this descends from the ears?
Or who are those scribes who record whatever many thoughts arrive?
And how is it that, in their multitude and in their multiplying upon one another, there is no turmoil among them, nor any confusion?
And this same pattern is seen in the working of the eye, which is astonishing.
And by this same means the mind reaches what is outside the body, and it draws visible things to itself and inscribes within itself their invisible forms,
as when someone sees a broad city that receives people through many gates. Now then, do all of them stay in one place? Surely not,
but some in the marketplace, some in houses, some in temples, or in the streets, or in the lanes, or in the inn, each of them stays, as each one wishes and as suits him.
And in this way I see that city of the mind which is established within us,
whose entrances from the senses are very many. And the mind distributes each of them and settles them in recognized places.
And just as we see, in likeness to the image we mentioned of the people of the city,
who have relatives and friends, and they enter that city not by one gate only,
yet on entering they do not become separated from their relatives,
and again, strangers enter by one gate, and when they have entered inside,
they scatter and do not gather with one another; in this way let us understand concerning the mind.
Chapter 10. And he spoke concerning the tenth chapter, that the mind performs its work by means of the senses. In this way behold that breadth of the mind,
for sometimes the knowledge of one thing only is gathered in us from many senses.

And in this way look at the breadth of the mind, for sometimes the knowledge of one thing is gathered in us even from many senses. And again, from one sense we understand many things, resembling one another in nature.

But let us liken it to some image, so that the statement we wish to make may become clear. Now, suppose we inquire about tastes, which is sweeter or which is more bitter, if we find the bitterness of gall and the sweetness of honey?

Now since this is clear, the discerning of this has been found, found under one sense, of things that are opposed to one another, by the separation of their dwelling by the mind [?], namely the sense of taste,
sight and hearing, touch and smell.
For when someone sees honey, and hears its name, and perceives its taste, and smells its scent, and tests it by touch, he recognizes that one thing through many senses.
And then again we have understood many things through one sense, namely hearing.

For it receives sounds of various kinds, mingled together, and the eye too receives many different colors, one and another: white and black and other colors as well, which are contrary to one another.
In the same way, tasting, smelling and touch each extend to many things that are opposed to one another.
Chapter 11. And he spoke concerning the eleventh chapter, that the nature of the mind is invisible. What, then, is the mind in its own nature,
in the power distributed among the senses, which has prior knowledge of things that come to be through each one of them?
And I think that no one among the intelligent would suppose or suspect that the mind is one of the senses.
For if the mind were a sense, it would have kinship with some one sense, because it is simple and not composite. And it is impossible for anything composite to exist in what is simple.

And this composition is attributed to the senses, and each one of them is separate and divided by its own function and not mixed with the others. Therefore the mind is indeed something other and not a sense, since it is simple and not composite.
And the apostle Paul said, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" But I say: who is there who has understood his own mind? So let those great talkers tell us,
those who claim to know the nature of the Godhead and think this makes them knowledgeable: have they understood themselves?

Have they examined the mind of their own minds? And if the mind is divided and composite, how can something intelligent exist in what is composite? Or how can it act within a mixture of elements that are opposed to one another?
Now then, is it simple and not composite? And how then was it divided among the separate senses?
And how did what is found [?] come to be in what is multiplied, and again what is multiplied in what is found [?]?

But I have come upon a matter at which I was astonished. When I heard that saying of God, when he says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," then an image is indeed complete and not lacking anything of the form found in the archetype, so that it may worthily be called an image.

But if it is found lacking in anything of the archetype, then for this reason it no longer has the image. And now, since the mind of God is inexpressible and incomprehensible, it must be that this is found in his image as well.

And if the archetype is inaccessible to knowledge, while its image is accessible to knowledge and known, then there is a clear difference between them, an irrefutable one, in the revealing of this saying. Now, when the nature of the mind cannot be depicted and cannot be expressed by knowledge, the truth of the image in relation to the archetype has been revealed, that is, to the nature of the Godhead,
which cannot be depicted and is incomprehensible, and to which our nature was made like.

Chapter 12. And he spoke concerning the twelfth chapter: an inquiry concerning the treasury of the mind, and a natural discourse concerning laughter and weeping. Let every mouth that speaks vainly be stopped, those who suppose that the power of the mind resides in certain members.
And some have said that it dwells in the heart. And they prove this by a worthless indication.
And those who have supposed that it resides in the heart prove it in this way, from the placement of the heart right in the middle of the body,
saying that from there the movement of the wills arises over the whole body, so that it may perform its own work.
And then, as proof of their statement, they adduce the arising of grief and anger, since these two evident things come forth from the heart.

And those who suppose that the mind resides in the brain have likened it to the tower of a city, in which the sovereign power is settled, ruling from on high over its people and surrounded by a multitude of servants.

In the same way they said of the mind that it dwells in the highest part of the body, which is the brain, and is surrounded by the sense organs as by servants. And as evidence for this they adduce the affliction that befalls the mind whenever some affliction strikes the brain, from wine or from anything else. And again, they have brought forward another figure concerning the brain and the heart. And some have said that the heart is akin to the mind through its warming motion,
For it is always in motion, like fire. Heat flares up from the heart, and for this reason the movement of the mind was joined to it.
And some have declared that the heart is the dwelling place of the mind, while others say that the membrane of the brain is where the senses gather.
And at times they affirm concerning the rational mind that it is in no other place than there where the ear is set, and in which the sounds that enter resound.
And the pupil that is planted in the eye brings in colors of many kinds, and the mind attains them, and the smell of many kinds of things is apportioned and distinguished by it.

And again, the sense of taste too is apportioned nearby by the same means, for it comes out from the membrane, from the sensory cord that leads out like a channel from the fingers [?], and from the cord that is joined there. For this reason they affirm what they say.

But I do not deny it. For sometimes nature is altered by afflictions that reach the brain, until it is held back from its proper activity by that natural cause and by that bodily affliction, when it takes control; and because the heat of the senses comes out from the heart,
for it is kindled toward motions, and the membrane of the head gathers the sense organs, in accordance with the statement of those who declare that the brain contains it and that vapor reaches it.
This I have heard from those who recount it, and I do not deny it,
but neither do I confirm this teaching, that the nature of the mind should be confined to one place.

For the alteration of the mind comes about not only from an affliction of the head, which befalls it from the various parts of the loins when these pain it, as the skilled physicians say, and they name that disease guarsam [?], because it is bound by a cord.
And as for what comes about from sorrow, it does not come from the heart, as is supposed, but is some affliction at the mouth of the stomach.

And in this way the skilled physicians, who minutely investigate the causes of diseases, say that the outgoing passages expand and contract at the onset of sorrow and joy, and by this means what has been held back by the breath passes out into the depth of the body.

But when the vessel and passage that holds the breath becomes narrowed, the breath sometimes bursts out of that narrowness by a natural rush and spreads into wider spaces. This is the cause of grief, and it is called a sigh. And the tightness of the heart that people think comes from this is not really in the heart,
but is something that happens at the mouth of the stomach,
when the bile that embitters the stomach overflows and squeezes it severely.

For this reason the face of those who grieve becomes yellow, like egg yolk, resembling [?], and this comes from the great outflow of bile from the veins of the upper part of the body. And our discourse has also made clear what lies in its opposite; I mean the matter from which gladness and laughter come.
For when a person hears some joyful matter, the passages of the body widen out from delight and joy.
and just as the fine passages narrow and the body's parts press together until the moisture rushes up to the head and to the membrane

inside it, and from the great pressure, as it builds up in the depths of the brain, it is pushed out through the passages to the eyes as the brows contract and draw together. The moisture comes down, drips, and becomes tears. Understand the rest in the same way.
When the passages widen beyond their usual measure, they take in air into that space, and then nature sends it out through the outlet of the mouth.
Because of this all the members are shaken, and above all the liver, at the exit of this air, and its exit is made easy also by the [?] of the cheeks.
And this is called laughter. And I do not say this to claim that the mind resides in the liver, nor yet, because of the blazing up of the heat of the blood in the heart at the time of anger,
would we say that the mind is located in the heart; rather, I say that these things belong to the condition of the body,
for the mind is settled in all the members equally, in like manner, according to the measure of each member, its mingling being by an inexpressible principle.

Although some cite that word of Scripture stating that the mind is in the heart, I shall accept their statement without examining it closely, for the one who mentioned the heart also joined the kidneys to it, when he said in the Psalm:
"God the righteous, who tests the hearts and the kidneys." And now we must say whether the mind dwells in both of them or in only one of them.
And if now the mind is held fast in the stirring of some disease that befalls a person,

this, then, is a clear indication concerning the mind, that it is settled in some member; nor does the affliction from which the inflammation of a member arises become an expeller of the mind. Now this account is a bodily one: that when something has settled in a vessel, it would no longer be possible for anything else to settle in it.
But the nature of the mind is neither sunk in the depth of the body nor expelled by the fatness of the flesh. Rather, the body was created like a musician's lyre.
And just as the lyre player cannot display the art of his playing because its strings are unserviceable, and the lyre becomes useless and idle, even though the musician is skilled,

In the same way the mind holds together the whole body and acts through each member according to that member's measure, as it has need. And when the body is sound by nature, the mind displays its power in it.
But as for that which is incapable of receiving the working of its wisdom,
the mind's trace becomes invisible in it, for the mind joins itself to that which stands firm in its own nature and flees from that which has been altered.
And I perceive in this a natural consideration, from which that reasoning, a subtle teaching, is learned.
For the perfection of those supreme good things is God, toward whom everyone who desires the good hastens.
For this reason we say that the mind is an image of the good, so long as it stands upon the beauty of the root, in likeness according to its power,
and it is in the good; but when it falls away from it, it is stripped of the beauty that was with it, and it becomes coarse and ugly.

And as we have said that it is adorned with the beauty of the root, which is the nature of the Godhead, and as a mirror shows the beholder the likeness of his image, in the same way nature becomes such when it is adorned by the governance of the mind.
Then it becomes like the mirror of the beholder. And if this body is held by it in [?], and its beauty then submits to it in all perfection, it appears adorned and truly established.
But when that union becomes estranged, and the superior submits to the inferior, and the heavy element remains alone, its ugliness appears, for the body alone is coarse and ugly.
It is not by the ugliness of this that the beauty of nature is destroyed, and the image of God no longer appears in it.
For when its beauty is removed far from nature, nature becomes like the back of a mirror, and then the ugliness of that gross body appears.
And thus the birth of evil comes about through the driving out of the good, and the good is that which is near to that first good, which is the root of the Godhead.
But that which does not resemble it is then undoubtedly far from it.
And if beauty is some one thing by which God is described, then the mind too has beauty and a nature. When it is kept by it, it becomes an image of that likeness.

And for this reason, know that this material body of ours stays firm as long as the mind governs it. But when it becomes estranged and separated from what holds it, and is removed from the boundary of good things, that material body is brought to ugliness by following its own will, which is turned away from good things.
But this inquiry of ours is the cause of what we were seeking earlier, namely: Does the nature of the mind reside in some one part of the body, or does it extend equally to all the members?

And now, behold, we have shown that the statement of those speakers is false who say that the hindrance of the mind from its own works comes about from every affliction that befalls the brain, which is the dwelling place of the mind; but our statement has been confirmed, in which we said that
the mind resides in all the members according to their measure and does its work with perfect governance, by the power of the mind.

But if some limb is injured, the mind can no longer move it by its direction, because of that occurrence of injury. And we have mentioned this for the following reason: that the mind is governed by God, and this material body by the mind, so long as we remain in accord with its nature.
And if it is changed from that state, that activity of the mind withdraws from it.

And let us return again to the same discourse and say that when the body remains in accord with its nature and does not change from it, the mind is then its governor. But if a limb is injured, from then on the mind no longer does its work, for that injured limb cannot contain it.

And it would be fitting for us to confirm this statement again with a clearer answer, if our discourse were not burdensome to the hearers; yet we still wish to bring in a little discourse to make this matter clear.

Chapter 13. And he spoke in the thirteenth chapter concerning sleep and yawning and dreams. For the life of those material, flowing ways is likened to the water of a river, into which a current is always brought from its source. And if its outlet is in a ravine or a hollow, it fills that place.
For that one place cannot hold the river back, but some of it flows out and some flows in.
So too is this life of [?], by movement and flow.
For these opposing material things are always moving and turning, and when their movement ceases, that life too ceases.
Just as satiety follows hunger and hunger again follows satiety, and sleep drives away the toil of weakness, and weakness in turn brings on that condition of sleep.
For none of them stays fixed in its own activity.
Rather, each one draws on its companion, and as one thus follows another, nature remains established in its own order.
And if living creatures remained forever in the toil of their existence, their limbs would be broken down by toil. And constant rest of the flesh stirs up [?] and brings on slackness.
But when nature receives both of these in measure, at a well-apportioned time, this becomes for it the power to endure through the alternation of opposites, as we have said.
And when the body grows weary from weakness and is then given rest by sleep,

it resembles those horses wearied from running, which afterward find rest. In the same way sleep carefully compels the body, so that the nourishment may be distributed through all the passages of the body without hindrance, and no toil may hinder its passage.
And just as moist earth gives off vapor when the radiance of the sun spreads over it, so it happens in our bodies when the nourishment is heated by the natural warmth.
And then that fine vapor rises and reaches the head, like smoke that strikes a wall.
And then that vapor is distributed in the passages of the senses, and the sense becomes idle from its work. And that vapor escapes from there.
And the closing of the eyes comes from the weight of the eyelid upon it, like lead.

And likewise the ears are filled with that vapor, like a house with its door shut, and this sense too ceases from its natural activity. And this is called sleep, on account of the dulling of the senses in the body, so that the way may be made smooth for the food and it may pass through all its proper passages.
And therefore, when the inner sense-organ is constricted by that vapor and its power is held back by that thickness.
Then the cords are naturally wrung, and what is wrung is squeezed by the constriction, as when a launderer wrings a garment.
And that place of the flesh is joined together by a multitude of cords, and when that vapor comes out of it,

It becomes thickened [?], because that vapor cannot get out of the places that are fashioned together all at once. Then what is left of it goes out through that [?]. This is called yawning: when the jaw opens wide [?] and the breath is drawn completely into the inner throat, so that it may carry out from there the residue of that vapor, which resembles the thickness of smoke. This happens mostly after sleep, when some residue of that vapor has remained.
And this too indicates that the mind is joined to nature,
for when a person is awake, the mind is in motion and its activity goes forward, but when nature inclines to sleep, the mind also remains idle and motionless.

However, if anyone supposes that the imaginings of dreams are the motion and activity of the mind in sleep, we say this: its true activity is that which takes place with wisdom and understanding, whereas what takes place in sleep is manifold imagining. This is a kind of likeness of the manifold activities of the waking mind, [?] from the animal-like soul [?], as it is imprinted.
For when the soul is left alone, apart from the senses, in sleep, it then undoubtedly becomes idle in its work of governing,
and when the senses are held back, the mind too is held back along with them from its own activity.

And the following fact gives proof of this. For sometimes a person sees in sleep that he is, as it were, taking part in some shameful and unseemly act, which he would not have touched if he were awake, when the mind governs the body with understanding;

But I think that the highest power of a person rests from the motion of the senses, while the nourishing part produces fancies in sleep. What it thinks about while awake, it practices and pictures again afterward. And the sleeper sees things in sleep that are neither true nor clear, but come through error and without understanding.
And just as in the body each member performs its natural function not for itself alone, but also for the other members that are joined to it, since they too suffer through its suffering,
so again it happens in the soul as well, for when one part is held at rest and another moves, the whole body too moves along with that part.
For what is joined by nature cannot be separated, those things that are joined by that power of nature from [?] the mind.
But when we are awake, the mind rules and the senses are its servants, and the body is not outside their governance; for the mind is harmful [?] to the food, and the senses are its receivers.

And we see the opposite of all this, in which the nourishing sleep sometimes brings the other [powers] to a halt, even though elsewhere they proceed openly. But since the nourishing power leads forth and activates the whole of nature, the power of sense does not on this account become idle, and it cannot be that everything
that is natural should be idle; but the activity of the senses is hidden when it is idle because of sleep.
And in like manner the mind has its beginning in the base [part], for when that is stirred, the mind is stirred with it, and when that subsides, the mind too subsides with it, in the manner of fire.
And when fire is kindled in chaff and the wind does not fan it, it neither goes out nor catches what is around it, but instead of flame it gives off smoke into the air.
But when the wind blows, its smoke turns into flame. So too the mind, when its activity in the senses is halted by sleep, grows sluggish,
and it can neither blaze up through them nor be entirely extinguished, but it moves feebly with an inferior activity.

And it is like a skilled [?] player of a stringed instrument: when the strings of the instrument are damp and slack, he cannot bring a harmonious sound from them, even though the player's hand acts with skill, because the strings do not sound as he wishes. Even if they give out a sound, it is not harmonious and beautiful, but unseemly.

So too is the lyre of the senses when it grows slack in sleep, for their mover has either subsided because of the fullness of the body, or else moves with a feeble motion, since its instruments are unable to receive the activity of their governor.

For this reason the vision is confused, and the foreknowledge belonging to wakefulness is obscured [?] by that doubt-inducing vision. Sometimes a dream announces something that is to come, for the fineness of the mind far surpasses the coarseness of the body. Therefore that which is seen in sleep,
its particular character is not easily explained clearly,
so that it would be true by likeness, and it comes about through fancy. Through such a fancy Pharaoh's cupbearer saw that he was pressing grapes into Pharaoh's cup.
Likewise the chief baker saw what seemed to be a basket standing on his head. Each of them saw what they used to do while awake,
for the vision held a foreknowledge of their affairs, and what they saw of the coming event was made known to the soul.
But if Daniel and Joseph and those like them knew the coming of events by divine power, this does not belong to the matters proper to what we are discussing.
Nor does it come from the power of dreams, and neither ought we to say that everything the saints saw while awake was according to the custom of nature and not a vision from God.
And just as all people govern themselves by their own mind, and few are made worthy of a vision from God,
so too all people by nature see dreams in sleep, and the chosen, those who are worthy, see a true vision in sleep.
And if Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and Nebuchadnezzar, ruler of Babylon, received from God knowledge of things to come, this was a divine dispensation.
It was somehow necessary that the hidden wisdom of the saints be revealed, so that people might not be ignorant of their great benefits.
And how would Daniel have attained his proper measure, if the priests and sorcerers had not been left ignorant of Nebuchadnezzar's vision?
And if Joseph had remained in prison, how would Egypt have been saved through his management? For sometimes what happens in dreams comes to resemble the conditions of the body.
For this reason the thirsty person sees himself moving about by rivers. So too the hungry person sees himself, as it were, receiving food. So too the young man burning with love,
sees what resembles his own arousal, and sometimes he even carries out that fantasy in deed during sleep.
I too have some small experience of a dream: I was once treating a sick man who was delirious.

And he was weighed down after taking some food. He began to cry out and shout, saying that his belly and his bowels were filled with a heavy thickness. At that time relief through sweating had come near to him.

And again he began to shout and cry out, saying that some men had poured cool water over him from a jug. It went on like this with him until his condition became clear, when a heavy sweat broke out and his bowels were loosened.
What the sick man could not tell us plainly, because of the affliction of his nature and the severity of the disease,
the sleeper was able to tell in sleep, apart from the disease, by the subtlety of the mind.
And so it is made known to us by skilled physicians that the matter of dreams gives signs in many ways according to people's diseases.
For the dream of one whose stomach aches is one thing, and the dream of those whose head aches is another; likewise,
those who have a full stomach have one kind of dream, and the melancholy and those with loosened bowels have another, for this reason:
that the nourishing power has a share of the rational power by being mixed with it,
and whatever disease dominates a person, the dream too is made to resemble it.
And again, dreams also occur according to people's ways of life, for the dream of the brave is one thing and that of the cowardly another,
and that of the virtuous is one thing and that of fornicators another, and that of the generous is one thing and that of the wicked another.

And it would be more fitting if someone were to say that these things, coming from the irrational part, remain with the soul in sleep by force of habit, just as a man while awake is settled in and occupied with his own business.

Chapter 14. And he spoke in the fourteenth chapter of how the mind does not reside in one part of the body, and of the distinction between spiritual and bodily movements. But we have passed over many things with which we were occupied, when we were inquiring about the mind, that it is not settled in one member,
but extends to all the members equally, and its motion in all the members is equal, according to the mind that is in it.
And sometimes the mind follows the movements of nature and becomes their servant.

For sometimes the nature of the body takes the lead, gains mastery, and brings on distress and joy. Their cause is a desire for food, or for some word that has entered the senses. Then the mind becomes, through subtle means, the procurer for the body of whatever the body has longed for and wanted. But this is found only among beast-like people,
who make the mind subject to the will of the flesh.
But among people who are perfect in virtue it is not so; rather, among them the mind is the leader in action and not a follower of that will, and for them it chooses the good with measure.

For we find three divisions in the power of life: the first nourishes without sense perception; the second nourishes with sense perception; and the third is perfect, endowed with speech and reason, and is adorned with those others.
And let no one suppose that there are three souls in the composition of man; rather, the perfect soul is one, the intelligent and incorporeal soul, mingled with the bodily nature.

Material nature is wholly subject to change and corruption. If there is a nourishing power in it, its movement is one of growth and increase. And if the power of life fails, its movement turns toward decay.
The power of sense perception does not exist without that material [?], nor does the intellectual power exist without sense perception.
Chapter 15. And he spoke in the fifteenth chapter concerning the soul: The rational soul is truly called soul,
while the others are called soul only by sharing the name. For every power of the mind is spread through the whole body, in each member according to their capacity.

And if some created beings are subject to the action of nourishment, and some [are moved], apart from the mind [?], by the power of the senses, then there is no beauty in the former and no mind in the latter. So let no one now suppose that souls are many,
for everything that exists, when it is perfect,

that to which it is attributed has the joy [?] that is called so in truth. But when the attribution to it does not hold in every respect, that attribution becomes void [?]. For example, when you see a true loaf, you say that this is a loaf of bread;
but when you see a loaf carved out of stones, having the form and colour and every property resembling that true loaf, yet it is not food,
it is not called a true loaf, but a loaf by resemblance, since it is made of stone.

Everything that does not truly have a name by nature is given that name by likeness. In the same way we say that the true and perfect soul is the rational one, and its perfection is speech. Even if there is something else besides this, it is called a soul only by likeness, and not truly a soul.

But the activity joined together [?] in living creatures is attributed to the soul. For this reason creation explained, concerning the acquiring of cattle for eating, that they should be like the green herbs of the meadows, for they are not far from the nature of plants, not even by the sense perception they have.

And since even the herb is nourished and grows without sense perception, let the lovers of the flesh understand this, and let their mind not be bound overmuch to visible, beastly things, but let them devote their desire [?] to the virtue of the soul.

And that the soul is true, we understand by means of it. But all the beasts, among perceptible things [?], cling to their own will in everything. But the length of the discourse and the inquiry has led us elsewhere, and we have left off,
That which we ought to have said beforehand: the matter of the mind in man, or the materiality of nature.
For we are asking in which of these the mind is in us, or in which member it abides.

We say that it is distributed through all the members, for it is not enclosed inside the body, but the body holds it from outside. For this is not truly said either of a water container or of any other vessel in which bodies are held.
But the union of the mind is inexpressible and incomprehensible, for it is inside. And the incorporeal is held by bodies from outside as well. For bodies are held by incorporeal things,

but the mind is united to nature in a manner unimaginable and inexpressible. And it [?] within it, and it is from it without being held back and without remaining, in a manner that we are unable to speak or tell.
But when nature stands firm, it also does its work under the governance of the mind.
But if some affliction befalls it, then the mind becomes grieved and lame.
But let us come to that same divine word which said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness."

Chapter 16. And he spoke concerning the sixteenth chapter, concerning the inquiry into what God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," and in it is the inquiry concerning the likeness: how the passible resembles the one who has no passion, and the mortal the immortal, and how male and female can exist among those who are in the likeness of God. For those outside wise men thought, when they attributed to the greatness of man a notion base and feeble, when it was heard
that man is like this great world, and that man is a small world within the great one, for the elements are found in him in their entirety.
And now those who glorify man with such great glory have, because of this name, forgotten that they are glorifying one whose properties are found even in gnats and mice,
for their constitution is mixed from these same four substances, and the nature of every green plant, or of every sentient creature, is from these same.

And some of these increase and some decrease. Tell, then, to what do they liken man, or for what reason: to the changeable heaven, or to the corruptible earth, or to those things that are between them, which are to pass away with the passing away of these two?
Or to what, then, is the greatness of man likened? To nothing among the created things of this world, but to the image of the Creator.
Now you will surely say: what then is this word spoken concerning the image, or how may the corporeal be likened to the incorporeal, or the transient to the eternal,

or how may the corruptible resemble the incorruptible and the changeable the unchangeable, or how may [?] the one raised in evil resemble the all-good? We see that likeness far removed from the true image,
for the likeness, when it resembles its original, upon which it was truly depicted, is then called image and likeness.
But if its likeness is far removed from the original, this is no longer called a likeness, but something else.
Now how is this man, a living, mortal and corruptible being, the image of that pure nature, without beginning, incorruptible and immortal?
But the divine word does not lie, for it says that the first man was created in the image of God; and yet weak human nature does not resemble the glory of God.
For these two matters each demand their own measure, when our nature is to be set alongside God.
Either corruption would have to be found in the Godhead, or corruption [?] in man, so that the statement about the image might be extended [?].

And now, if we are subject to passions and pains, and God is above these things, is there then some other account left by which we may understand that word of God which says: "Let us make man in our image and likeness"?
Let us also recall what follows in this holy book and investigate it, in case we may perhaps understand from there and come to know the truth.
And afterward, when it had said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," and for what reason this was, let us then recall this statement as well:
"And God made man; in the image of the Godhead he made them; male and female he made them." We said before, and we say now, that this saying was spoken to refute the heretics, so that you may know
that the Only-begotten Son made man in the image of God, so that we should not divide the Godhead of the Father and of the Son,
for when the scripture named God as the maker of man, the one who was said to be like him.
But let us set this matter aside for now and return to the same question we were investigating: how this man is weak and raised in affliction, while God is glorious, and yet man is called like him.
Now then, let us investigate the statement thoroughly, for we find that the man who was like God was another, and not this present one raised in affliction.
"God made man; in the image of God he made him."

Now then, the creation of that which was made was completed, and it again added to this and said: "Male and female he made them." But I think that everyone knows that female and male are outside that root, as the Apostle said:
"In Christ there is neither male nor female."
But in this it mentioned the division of man. Now then, our creation is twofold.
One part is made like God, and one part is divided. For the statement thus speaks of the connection of what was said:
For it first said: "God made man; God made him in the image of God," and after this it said:
"Male and female he made them," and this is far from being conceivable in the Godhead.
But this is what I think: it is a great teaching found in the holy Scriptures.
These two forms are very far apart from each other, and man is between them. I mean the divine, incorporeal nature and the brute, irrational animal.
For in the nature of man there is found something proper to each of these two natures. From the Godhead come reason and understanding. In it there is no male and female.
These are found in human life. But we have learned from scripture that the rational element is because of it [?]. After that, the likeness of the brute animals came upon man.
But first he said that "man was made in the image of the Godhead," as the apostle said:
"In him there is neither male nor female." What then is the meaning of this? Let no one blame me if I have eagerly established this with an argument that can be understood.
For however often men call God good, he is above all goodness.
Man was created only for the sake of goodness. Since this is so, our nature was created for this reason. When he created it, he did not create it lacking anything, and he made something good in it,
which is in it. That good is not a body but the fullness of good things

that he created in it when he created man from non-being into being, and brought what had not existed into existence. He made it lacking in no good thing, for those good things are very many and countless.
For this reason the word of Scripture gathered all of it together when it said, "In the image of God he made him."
And this saying is like what would be said if one were to say that he made him full of every good thing.
And if God is the fullness of good things and this one is his image, then in good things is he indeed like that root?
And now, then, is there indeed in us every good thing and every virtue and every grace and every wisdom and every adornment of good?
First of all there is this freedom: that man is not enslaved but has authority, acting according to his own will,
For nothing that is under compulsion and constraint has freedom in it. Freedom is this: to have authority over one's own will. For if the beauty of the image lacks anything, it is not an image.
But there is one thing that separates divinity from humanity: that the one is creator and the other is created.
And upon this distinction there follows in turn for each a different property, for we believe that the uncreated nature is unchangeable from its own order forever.

But the created does not exist except through change on account of it, for it was not made until change came about; it did not come to be [?] and motion, when the Creator by his grace changed it from non-being into being.
And just as the Gospel speaks of that image of Caesar which was on the gold, an image which was like the king in form and different from him
in material, so also here, in place of that image, I understand what is in the nature of divinity and what is in that of humanity,
in which there is likeness and a distinction of natures, I mean of creator and created; for the one always stands and will remain forever.
But what is created began with change, for it did not exist and then came to be. For this reason it was open to turning aside,
for scripture says that when the Creator knew by foreknowledge,
that this man was going to have authority and walk according to his own will, and that he was also going to turn aside, as indeed happened,
then he fashioned upon that image of his maleness and femaleness, which are not in that root but, as we have said, are close to the nature of the beasts.

no one knows the reason for their creation except those who were eyewitnesses of the Word, and the grace given to them. But we, according to our ability, speaking by likeness and conjecture, will say what comes close to that true account, as it has been given to our tongue by a revelation of the mind to those
who will receive it with a good mind. For when it was said that "God created man," this pointed to humanity only in general, and the created individual was not included with it,
but the scripture mentioned the name of Adam, as it said, only afterward, and did not give the created individual the name of humanity,

But "humanity" is the term that gathers together every kind. Now therefore, by this comprehensive name let us understand that that first explanation was a statement concerning what properly belongs to the nature. For it is not fitting for us to say that anything could be left undetermined by God in all its fullness.

And just as when someone has spoken of a certain person, even if you have not disclosed the name, you have nevertheless made plain the definition of the man, with all his adornment and stature and whatever signifies his body, so too, I think,
that the fashioning of one man is the completeness of humanity in every part, by the power of that work of his.
[?] and whoever shall arise at the last end of the world, among all of them will be that first image.

For this reason one man is called all, for in the power of God nothing is past and nothing is to come, but everything stands before him. Although we wait for it in hope, yet with God it is unfailing and stands firm.
