For the nature as a whole, from the first to the last, exists in one image. But the division into male and female was created, I think, for this reason: for the establishment of the race.
Chapter 17. And he spoke concerning the seventeenth chapter [?]: what we should answer to those who inquire about propagation and childbearing,

whether it came about after the sin, and, if man had not sinned, where the souls would have come from. What shall we answer to those disputers who say to us: "Why did birth come about after the transgression, or where would the generations have come from, if those first humans had remained without transgression?"
But before inquiring into this present subject, it is better that we obtain a refutation of the words of those who oppose us.

For they say that before the transgression there was no birth, nor had the womb been opened for offspring. But when they were cast out of paradise after the transgression, and after the punishment and retribution of that woman,
and by the affliction and pain of childbirth, which she deserved, then Adam knew his wife, and from then on they began to bear children.
Now, since there was no marriage in paradise, nor knowledge of the marriage bed, nor childbirth, and they did not transgress under compulsion, surely generations would not have come to be.
And if that grace of life had not been brought to death, and marriage had not come to be a way for the continuance of nature,
by which came the entry of many in place of those two who had gone out, so that that sin became a gain for the human race,
then, if not, only those two first ones would have remained, had nature not been moved to produce generations in order to overcome death.
But the plain meaning of that statement is known to those who are counted with the apostle Paul, who have attained to the mystery of paradise.

Now this is what we have to say on this matter. When the Sadducees, those deniers of the resurrection, rejected it, and put forward their argument to him, and mentioned the resurrection, and brought forward that woman as an example, then the Lord answered and gave understanding not only to the Sadducees but to all who oppose that incorruptible life.
Concerning the resurrection he said: "For in the resurrection they neither marry
nor are given in marriage," for death no longer has any right to rule over them, for they are like the angels and are sons of God,
when they have become sons of the resurrection.

For the grace of the resurrection proclaims to us nothing other than a return to the very place from which we were first cast out. For this grace is the way back to that first life: dwelling again in Paradise, from which we went out.
Then those who live will be like angels.
And the indication of that first life, that it was like the life of the angels, was made known to us by this: that at our return our life will become like the life of the angels.
And now among the angels there is no marriage, and yet they are very numerous and form many hosts, as Daniel tells us in his vision. And if we had not fallen away from the order of the angels,
in which we were at first, and had not been changed from the likeness of the angels, then we would have had no need
for our multiplication to take place through marriage; rather, just as the multitude of the angels exists without this, and that is beyond devising and beyond understanding,
so too it would have been among those who, by the dispensation of the Creator, have been made a little lower than the angels.
But if anyone is perplexed in mind when inquiring into the existence of souls, had the bond of marriage not been laid upon man,
let us then ask about the state of the being of the angels: how is it that they are of one nature and yet counted in a very great multitude? This is our answer to the matter:
just as they are many without marriage, so too with humans; for the return of humans to the order of the angels at the resurrection indicates that they will indeed be like the angels.
And now let us come to the original question: how is it that, when God made man in his own image, he fashioned maleness and femaleness?
This is what we were saying earlier: that he who created all things, and man wholly in his own likeness and image,
it was not fitting that the completion of the soul should be seen only once it had reached its measure,
But through that foreknowing account it was quickly seen what human nature was going to become.
And he glorified it with that glorious glory of the angels, for he saw it by foreknowledge.

that the will of man would be unsteady toward the good, and that the multitude of human souls, made a little lower, was going to fall from the glory of the angels, when it fell from the order of the angels.

Chapter 18. He spoke about the eighteenth chapter as follows: the brutish impulse rooted in us comes from our kinship with the beasts. In the same way, in this life of growth and increase, it was stamped on the nature of those
who were changed. In place of the glory of the angels, this brutish growth and increase was planted among them.
And I think that it is on account of this that David the prophet recalled the wretchedness of human nature and said:
"Man was in honor and did not understand." He gave the name of honor to that likeness to the angels, and for this reason he said that man's state is worse than that of the beasts,
which have no reason. He truly became like them,
for he is beastlike who changed that life by his inclining toward material things.
And from this I think that those many passions enter human life for this reason:
because we are not far removed from them at all. And the witness to this is that the ailment which is found among the irrational animals is found among us as well.
It is not right to say that this affliction in us came from our likeness to the Godhead.

But the life of the brute beasts had been made beforehand in the creation of which we spoke earlier, the pattern of its causes [?]. And so man acquired a way of generation like that of the beasts, and because of this the other things too
that are in their nature were joined to him.

For the anger found among humans cannot be likened to the image of the Godhead. Nor is it fitting to ascribe to that glorious nature any love of pleasure, or cowardice arising from any fear, or any rashness, or the love of greed, or hatred of being dishonored.
All these, and things like them, are far removed from the likeness of the Godhead.
Rather, man drew all these to himself from that animal part.
For everything that animal life acquired for the preservation of its kind, and whatever was thoroughly mixed into it, was transferred to man and remained in him in this way:

for flesh-eating animals are to be feared because of their wrathfulness; and those that bear many young are lovers of desire; and cowardice and timidity save the cowardly; and timidity saves them from the strong; and gluttonous eaters are distressed in a time of scarcity.
All these things and others like them were joined to human nature from the animal kind. An image,
which is painted by skilled painters so as to astonish people,
showing two images in a single head. In the same way, I think, the likeness in man is twofold.
the exactness [?] of the mind is divine, for it has been made like the beauty of the Godhead. For the form in which that ailment has settled has been made like the animals.
For at times irrationality follows, through the tendency toward fellowship with the beasts, until the evil covers over the good.
For if anyone turns the work of the mind toward such things, and forces himself to become a slave to such passions,
From then on a change of the image into the likeness of animals came about, until the whole nature came to resemble the form of animals.

And it is reason that acquires these through that enslavement, and it makes what is small appear great. For when reason assists the passion by its own activity, the brood of those evils increases greatly. The love of pleasures has done the same: its beginning came from that bestial fullness [?],

but in man's sin it grew, until many occasions of desire were born from it, such as cannot exist even among the beasts. And likewise, the fierceness of anger is akin to that of all the beasts, but it grows through the pursuit of deliberate intention; through the impulse of anger it cannot be changed [?]. And its dissolution is like that swollen bubble which, in time of rain, is seen on the waters for an instant and at once bursts, as though it had never been, when reason does not assist it. In this way, and in like manner, greed arises in what people do.
And the greed of swine and the pride of horses became the beginning of wantonness among human beings, and so too the other causes of beginning from the animal nature.
And when the mind assisted it, it became evil. And in the same way reason: when the mind changes such a movement within it, each one of these becomes a virtue.
And anger is changed into courage and divine zeal, and cowardice becomes caution, and timidity becomes obedience, and hatred becomes separation from evils.
And the power of the love of desire it changes into true goodness, and self-restraint lifts it above unseemly things, so that it may not be enslaved to evils.
And the great apostle praises such forbearance when he says that we should look nowhere but upward.
And so we find that every rational movement, by this glory, is made like the beauty of the divinity,
but the inclination of sin is heavy and brings one down to the depths.
And sometimes the one prevails more, for the mind of the soul more quickly accomplishes the drawing down below than the lifting up from the earth into [?] the air, because of that heaviness.

And sometimes our poverty fails to perceive the divine goods that are within us, when that beauty has come to be upon the image of the divinity made like passion, just as a beautiful [?] form is clothed in the ugliness of the passion of the body; the text literally reads "an ugly face clothed in ugliness." Now these, indeed, are subject to pardon,
who see this and then inquire into the divine nature, and can see nothing from this, and do not accept this saying.
But you may see this among those who have acquired virtue; you may see the image of God and his likeness,

for a man is unseemly in the flesh, if [?] he had been adorned with that divine beauty. So too, again, the one who is glorious in virtue and spotless of passions will confirm your mind for you concerning the divinity.
But it is better that one be made like the image. And who has rescued from evils the beauty of the mind of Jeconiah,
or of anyone else remembered for evil? But the image, truly preserved, was found unstained in Moses and in those like him.
And those in whom beauty remained undefiled are witnesses to our word that man was made in the image of God. But perhaps someone may be ashamed
when he sees that our nature, like the beasts, takes food and drink, and for this reason he is unwilling to say that man was made in the image of God.
But let him look for its complete dissolution, and let him look for that life which we hope to receive, as the apostle said: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink," and again:
"Man shall not live by bread alone" -- as the Lord said -- "but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God."
And the resurrection also declares to us that the life to come will be angelic.
And now, since the angels are without food, this is enough for understanding that man will be freed from that service when he reaches the measure of the angels.

Chapter 19. And he spoke, in the nineteenth chapter, concerning those who say that the delights of the good things in the world to come will consist of foods and drinks, because in the beginning man was commanded to live by these two. If someone should say: Why will man not return again to that same tree of life, since at first we lived by food, and why will he not be in it again?
But I, when I hear from the book of the prophet, understand that food as not merely bodily, nor that delight as human,
but as another food, apart from the bodily, whose delight reaches the soul alone, as Wisdom said,
"Let the hungry eat his bread" and "The Lord will gladden the hungry": this is the hunger. And again he says: "Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink!"
And again the glorious Isaiah says to those who are able to hear that beautiful saying of his: "Drink joy." And if he has also promised hunger as a punishment for those who deserve vengeance,
then he did not speak of that hunger as a lack of bread, nor of thirst as a lack of water, but as a lack of hearing the words of God.

And since God planted paradise in Eden, and Eden is translated as "delight," it is fitting that its fruit, by which man is nourished, should be such that its enjoyment is unchanging and does not pass away, as these enjoyments here pass away.
And it was said: Eat of every tree that is in paradise; eat for food.
Who will give to the one who truly hungers that tree encompassed with every good, which is in paradise, which is called by the name "All," the eating of which creation has permitted?
For by that generic word, which gathers together every form of good, it was also called "All."
Who would be nourished by the taste of that tree of double constitution? And I do not think that those lovers of learning would remain ignorant
of what that "All" is whose fruit is life, and again what this doubly mixed thing is whose measure is death.
For he who granted man the delight of all those good things, apart from [?], by a dispensation concerning the flesh and by mercy made man with a preparation of his constitution [?].
And I think that David and Solomon, both teachers of the interpretation of that knowledge, reckon it as one good.
And this is the beginning of delight, which is the good of truth. And that good is the "All."
For David said: "Let us delight in the Lord." And Solomon mentions wisdom, which is the Lord, and names it the tree of life.
So now the force of the word is one, whether you say "tree of life" or that tree which is called "All," whose taste is for created beings as the image of God [?].
And against that tree stands another tree, whose taste is the knowledge of good and evil,

for it bears fruit from opposites, each one within the other; but that fruit is mixed, flowering through that combination, and is distorted [?] in its nature. From this the Originator of life held man back.
And the serpent urges the eating of it, in order to prepare the paths of death.
And he persuaded the woman of his counsel, for he adorned that fruit with many-colored flavors, and it was beautiful to the sight, so that by that tasting she might grow accustomed to eating it.
Chapter 20. And he spoke concerning the twentieth chapter: What is that life which is in paradise, and what is that tree from which they were held back? What then is the tree
in which there is the knowledge of good and evil, mixed and flowering from the flavors of things perceived by the senses?
Now are we then to be found far from knowledge and true discernment when we inquire with a pure heart, in order to know what the knowledge of good and evil is?
For some say that knowledge in this place, as scripture says, is not understanding, but a distinction between understanding and knowledge.
For the discerning of good from evil is like this: as the Apostle says, it comes from a mature condition and from refined minds.

And for this reason these also command us to discern everything, and above all to discern what is spiritual, as he said. But "knowledge" never signifies something like science and skill, but rather those things toward which one should incline, as it is said:
"God knows those who are his," and as was said to Moses: "I know you above all."
And the one who knows all things says to the wicked: "I never knew you."
But the knowledge by which that mixed tree is known, this tree whose fruit was forbidden to them, is mixed of opposites, and the good is its helper.
And perhaps evil does not appear stripped bare, as it is in its own nature.
And if evil were naked, it would be rejected by everyone, if it were not covered with some covering of good, which attracts and seduces,
for the nature of evil is mixed: hidden anger dwells within it, while outwardly it shows the appearance of good. Lovers of silver think that silver is good and beautiful in color.
But "the root of all wickedness is the love of silver."
And whoever falls into the foul mire of fornication thinks that its taste is good and desirable,
and likewise in every sin, destruction lies hidden,
for most people count as good whatever pleases the senses.
But of the good, some is truly good and some is only supposed to be good.
For this reason God called this desire, which is supposed to be good, the knowledge of good and evil; by that knowledge he signifies the mixture and union of the two.
So then, evil is not merely evil undiluted, but is concealed within the good. Nor is the good good in a pure and separate state,
For the evil is hidden within it, and it is a mixed fruit; tasting it leads to death whoever approaches it. And Scripture cries out and says
that the true good is simple and not compound by nature, far removed from everything compound and joined together.
But evil is divided in many colors: it is supposed to be one thing, and when tested it turns out to be another.
And that knowledge is, as it were, the testing of it; it is, as it were, the beginning of death and corruption.

For this reason the serpent showed that evil fruit of sin not as the evil it is by nature. Otherwise he could not have seduced the human being with an evil that was plainly visible; instead he adorned it with beauty to look at and produced in the senses some slight taste.
And with this he seduced the woman, when she perceived the taste, as Scripture says: The woman saw that the tree was good for food and beautiful
to behold, and she took of its fruit and ate." And that eating was the parent of death for human beings.
And this is the mixed fruit, as the word revealed to the mind, and for this reason he named that tree the knowledge of good and evil,
that it is like those deadly poisons which are mixed with honey and are fair to look at. It is sweet to the taste and is thought to be good, and yet it is destructive to those who approach it.
And it is worse than anything, for this venomous thing has shown its trace.

For this reason also that man, lofty in his deeds and glorious in his name, the likeness of the nature of the Godhead, has become like vanity, as the prophet says. Now therefore the good that is among us is akin to that likeness.
But the affliction and distress that our life contains are estranged from the likeness of God.

For evil is not able by its own power to overcome the might of God, nor does the weakness of our nature prevail over the wisdom of God. How could it be possible for what is corruptible, being subject to change, to be stronger than what is eternal?
But neither does it admit any means of change, for the likeness of God stands firm in every respect,
whereas this corruptible nature of ours is unstable, not even remaining fixed in the good.
For that which is always in motion, if it keeps turning within the good, is engaged in an endless activity, since its advance is not stopped by any limit that it may seek.
But when it reaches the end, it will cease from motion.
And if it turns away from the good, makes its will evil, and reaches the end of evil,
then that unresting motion, when it finds no wide court left toward evil, turns back to the good.
For evil ceases once it has gone as far as its end.

When this has happened, then the coming of the good [?], and likewise, as we said, the unresting motion of our nature hastens toward the good; through the memory of the evil that befell it, it takes care not to turn back again to such a thing,
for our return to the good will take place when that nature of evil ceases at the limit of necessity.
And as the skilled astronomers say, this earth is filled with light, and darkness is a covering shadowed by the body of the earth.
And this comes about because it is like a ball, on the upper side, from behind the disk of the sun, in the shape of a cone.

For the sun is greater and wider than the earth by many parts, and it encompasses the earth with its radiance, until the light gathers together from the tips of the cone. And now I will give an illustration:
If you could reach the end of the light, then you would see it unbroken by darkness. In the same way we must understand it in our own case too,

for when we have gone out from the limit of evil and have reached the end of that darkness of sin, then after that we shall live in a light brighter than the eye of the sun by countless parts. And paradise will stand again, and there will be that tree which is called All,
and that is the tree of life.

And again, the grace of the image and the glory of dominion will no longer be as they are now, subjected to the necessities of life, as I suppose; rather, I await another kingdom, whose creation is hidden.

Chapter 21. And he said in the twenty-first chapter that the assurance of the resurrection is to be awaited through the multiplying of examples, one after another, more than through the saying of the Scriptures. But let us keep to the same discourse in which we were engaged, lest someone, out of desire for that sweetness
which we await, should regard the delay of those good things to come as a loss and a lessening [?],
those things which are above the understanding of natures and beyond speech, and should so regard the prolonging of the times of its arrival.
Now let him not become faint-hearted, like children who do not quickly receive what they ask for.
And all the more since everything is without doubt ordered with wisdom and knowledge, for nothing is outside providence and wisdom.
And perhaps you will ask what this dispensation is by which we do not at once attain what we long for and are not transferred from this life of distress.
But this bodily life, the completion of all things, has been extended by measure, until it is released from this yoke and reaches again that life of leisure and repose, of peace and joy.
But if this question must be examined, then let it be found out in accordance with true justice. What comes to our mind, however, is this.
And now let us return again to that same first saying: "Let us make man in our image and likeness.
And God made the man; in the image of the Godhead he made him."
Now the image of God, which is seen in all human nature, has been completed, but Adam does not yet exist, for Adam is translated "earthly," as we have heard from the Pharisees of the Jews.
And the Apostle, since he was trained in Jewish teaching and was thoroughly versed in their discourse, for this reason gave that man his name and said: The first man is from the earth, dust.
And God made the man in the image of the Godhead, a complete nature. He made him by that wisdom which prevails over all, and not over a part of the whole,
But in a single moment he saw the whole fullness of nature, he "in whose hand are all the ends of the earth," as the prophet says.
He saw it, he who knows all things before they come into being. He saw its two inferior parts,
which incline toward evil, and the two that are seen by their own will to share with the angels.
And that it would become contemptible. For this reason he mingled something animal-like into the nature of man,
for in the good divine nature there is no division into male and female.
Rather, he joined to human beings the property that the creation of the animals has.
For the glory of our creation was higher, since when he made man, he did not then say, "Increase and multiply," but only when he had divided male and female.
Only then did he say, "Multiply and have dominion over the earth." And this was not by the property of the divine nature,
but on account of the animal element, as Scripture said,

that this was said by God, "Increase and multiply," earlier to the creatures that move below. And if this had been said to man before the division into male and female, we would by no means have needed this animal-like birth.
But he saw this by foreknowledge, I mean the completion of humankind, who were destined to pass through this life.
Time was brought in by necessity, so that there might be that number of souls

which it received, so that they might enter the world, for he sees what is distant as if it were near, so that their completion might be the cessation of the times, which are to come to rest from that flowing motion,
since humanity was unstable within it. But when this begetting of human beings is ended and completed, the times too will be completed along with it.
Then there will be the renewal of all things and the transformation of all things, and that humanity, corrupted because of the earth, will be changed into that beginningless incorruption.
And I think that the apostle was referring to this idea in those words that he writes to the Corinthians:
"Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all fall asleep, but not all shall be renewed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at that last trumpet.
The trumpet will sound." And I think that when it is fulfilled and made complete according to the appointed measure, and nothing is lacking to that number of souls,
then in an instant the change of all will take place. And he called that time a moment and the twinkling of an eye.
But when the trumpet, the awakener of those who sleep, sounds for the resurrection,
then those who remain in this life will be like those renewed in the resurrection, and they will become incorruptible,

when this heaviness of the flesh no longer drags this body down to the earth. Rather, through its fineness it will become able to travel through the air, caught up by a cloud in the air, and from then on they will be with the Lord forever.
So this time, in its long-suffering, is suited to the increase of humankind,
for those who are of the measure of Abraham wished to look upon those good things and sought wholeheartedly that heavenly dwelling, as the apostle says.

But until now they are still seeking that grace, for God foresaw it with foreknowledge and "provided something better," as the apostle said, "so that apart from us they should not be made perfect." If they endure the delay, far from the reward,
they who saw those good things not by hope [?], but as the apostle said, and kept hold of that expected delight by trusting in the one who promised it.
then what indeed shall we do about the many who have some hope for good things [?] departed in the life of the soul, which has passed away?
And he confesses the reason for his longing in the psalm, when he said: "My soul longs and faints to remain in the courts of the Lord."
For he chose to be cast down in another [?]. For that other one said, who is among those who chose to remain in the dwelling of sinners rather than that life.
But above all this they were to attain [?], and to the delay, and to being entrusted to that dwelling. For a little of that delight is better than a thousand years of life,
"for one day in your courts is better than those thousands." And that dispensation was not to be revealed,
which he planned and spoke of, saying: "Human beings have been entrusted only to this hope of good things."
And for this reason he said at the end in the psalm: "Lord, God of hosts, blessed is the man who trusts in you." Now therefore it is not right for us
to become faint-hearted because of the delay of what we hope for; rather, let us become eager,

so that we may not be found fallen away from our hope. And as some ignorant person said, that in the time of summer there is a ripening of fruits, and the storehouses are full, and every good food abounds on the table.
And whoever considers this saying to be the whole of the matter is foolish and mad. Rather, it is necessary for us
to sow the seed and to provide beforehand the help by which its fruits may become fair. For, whether one wishes it or does not wish it, that time will arrive in its own season;
and he will see alike both the one who has been prepared for the increase of those fruits and the one who has remained idle at that time.
So also, I think, since the matter of the resurrection is now manifest, when the Lord says that the time of the change is coming, [?] to inquire into the times, as he says:
"It is not for you to know the years and the times." And let not weak minds conceive of the hope of the resurrection according to their own weakness,
but let one be diligent, through the hope of good deeds, to be an acquirer of those coming delights.

Chapter 22. And he spoke, in the twenty-second chapter, about those who ask: If the resurrection is good and sweet, why has it not happened already? Why do we wait for it after many ages? And if anyone who sees the course [?] of this world going on under its own ordering, by which the extent of the ages becomes known, says that it is impossible for what was mentioned before to be credible, and that these things will never cease from their motion, he has shown that he is an unbeliever.

For it is God who created the heavens and the earth in the beginning. But how do we understand that "by the word of the Lord the ages were established," as the apostle said, given that these visible things were once invisible?
With this same faith, then, shall we accept the word of God which says that this world stands by necessity, and shall we then give up the inquiry?
For there our faith has been brought to completion, made manifest by what has happened; and let us give up the search for what we cannot attain.
For it was easy to investigate the many causes and to explain them to those who profess this.
And those opponents are able to undo it with the labor of faith, until the saying about this coarse world is no longer conceivable.
True is what the Scriptures say, that all things were created by God. For those who oppose that saying speak thus: that material things are without beginning together with God. And they say further:
If God is a simple nature, without density and quantity, neither a body nor composite nor contained as bodies are,
and every material thing is known by its limit, and whatever falls under the senses
is known by color and shape and "bone" [?] and roughness and other things that are known through the senses, none of which can exist in the nature of God:
Now how is it possible for material things to come from things that do not exist, from things that do not change, and for this to become a changeable nature? And if you understand
that this comes from them, you will learn that it is found in them through that ineffable word.
And if matter is from them, how is that immaterial in which materiality too exists?
And likewise all the existing things through which the material nature is made known to us.
And if there is materiality in the Godhead, how is it uncompounded, simple and indivisible? Until one comes to coarseness [?], when material things come from him,
or one departs from this and says that this coarseness [?], which is matter,
he brought from outside and made these creatures from it.
And if it is outside God, then it is something other, apart from God, according to the measure of the account of its own properties.

And so there would be two beginnings without origin, to be conceived together and prepared together by providence [?], upon which judgments come and upon which reason would compel one to say this: that alongside the unoriginate Creator of all there was that unoriginate matter, as the wicked Mani said, and he would take the firebrand [?] of matter and set it in opposition to God.
And when we heard from Scripture that everything is from God, we believed.

and how much more [?] not concerning God, and no longer to inquire into it, for it is beyond our words. For we know that God is able to do all things and has power over all things, and that he changed their states according to his own will. And just as the power of God was able
to create created things out of nothing and likewise to establish the things that exist, so the power of God is able to build them again.
And our faith in this is not far from the truth.
For we would be able to persuade those whom the much-speaking one [?] concerning material things, so that they may not suppose that the argument has fallen short on this account.

Chapter 23. And he spoke in the twenty-third chapter about those who confess a beginning of the world, that even unwillingly it is incumbent on them to confess its end as well. And now it is no longer needful for us, with this argument of ours, to inquire further and again concerning material things, of which it has been proved that they have indisputably been newly brought forth by mind,
for we see all material things found to be separated from quality, and from the firebrand [?] by expression.

And its expression is by the bringing forth of the mind and not of bodies. And if you should speak of certain animals, or of plants, or of anything else whose standing is from matter, one has seen great division in the body.

And it is evident that each of them does not unite with another, for the definition of color is one thing, that of matter another, and the quality of things perceived by the senses is another by definition,
for smallness [?] and length and others like these are unmixed with one another, and with the body too they are by themselves unmixed,
for each of them has its own determined definition of what it is, and does not unite with any other visible thing that is inexpressible as regards quality.

But if color and solidity are created things, as are quantity and the properties of all the others, and if any one of them is removed from anywhere, each with its own definition, the body would be dissolved. And now you know that the separation of these dissolves the body, and their union makes it firm. So the body cannot stand when color is separated from it, or height, or extension and contraction, or matter, or any other single one of these properties. For when any one of these is found alone, it is not a body. Rather, it is mind that governs them, and the nature of the Godhead is intellectual. And it is not surprising if these intelligible and perfect things were created by the mind of the Godhead, which made these causes to establish bodies. And that is true mind, not like these intelligible natures.

And it brought about their establishment through their union with one another. But we have arranged our discourse in this way so that we may not return again to those same arguments, and so that the faith may suffice us, by which we believe that God brought forth these creatures from nothing and changed them into another order, as we hear from the Scriptures; and we believe this without any doubt.

Chapter 24. In the twenty-fourth chapter he gave a reply to those who say: "Matter is without beginning, together with God." And there is no need for our words to examine matter at length [?]. This shows that matter has a beginning, that it was begun by mind, and that mind is invisible. For we see that all material things are made up of quality, and when matter is stripped of quality, it can no longer be known by reasoning. And each of the qualities is made evident by [?] through reasoning, and reasoning is by the mind and not by the flesh. And how might you speak of some things, whether in animals, or plants, or in any other things whose existence is by means of matter? You would see a great distinction among them in their definitions.

And each of them is recognized as not being mixed with another. For the definition of color is one thing and is far from the definition of weight, and again the definition of touch is another. Softness and length and other such things do not mix with one another, nor with body, in their definition.

For each of them has a manifest definition of what it is and does not mix with another, and these things are seen in the account of quality. For color is perceived by the understanding, and solidity is known. And as for the quality and the remainder of each of all of them, whenever any one of them is withdrawn with its whole definition, the body is thereupon dissolved. And now you know that whatever comes to separation dissolves the body, and its union undoubtedly makes it firm. So the body does not stand when color, firmness, solidity, smell and corporeal form [?] are separated from it. And neither the remainder of each of them, nor each one of them, is a body when it is found alone.
But the seeing of these is by the mind, and the Godhead in its own nature, again by the mind and not by the eye, you would understand only with great difficulty,
so that this surpassing intelligible thing would be created by the mind of the Godhead, which made these causes for the firmness of the body.
And that intelligible thing is outside those minds that can be understood. He created its existence so that it would exist through the union of one with another.

But we have done this deliberately, so that we may not again turn our discourse away from the faith that we have believed: that God raised up this world from nothing, and afterward will change it and bring it to its own measure beyond this one, as we hear from the Scriptures and know without any dispute.

Chapter 25. And he spoke in the twenty-fifth chapter of how those who reject the Law might accept what the Scriptures say about the resurrection, lest perhaps, when someone sees these bodies dissolved,
he should liken the power of the Godhead to this as well and say that resurrection is not possible, as some say.

But this will give him a true indication for believing what is said, the word of the narrator. And the truth of this comes from the words he spoke, which he spoke and accomplished in deed, just as he said.
For the divine Scripture has spoken many words, and by this we know whether that word is true or false.
Let us look at the resurrection in the same way:
if those other things that were said were false and outside what is right, then surely these too are false.
And if the others bear witness through experience to the truth of what was said, then surely that other thing too, the account of the resurrection, must be held credible.
And now let us recall one or two of the earlier sayings that have been truly manifested, and let us understand that the word about the resurrection is true.
And now, who does not know this: that the sons of God formerly shone brilliantly with light and stood against all the kings of the earth,

and how their kings were in Jerusalem, and how strong [?] were the walls of that city? And what the towers were like, and the greatness of the construction of that temple, so that even the disciples of the Lord were amazed and begged the Lord to look upon it with amazement, as the holy Gospel says.
But the Lord informed them what was going to happen to that beautiful building:

desolation and complete disappearance. And they marveled at this. And then he said: A little while longer, and nothing of it will remain. And at the time of the Passion those women followed who were mourning the unjust judgment that the Jews passed upon him, for they did not know what dispensation was going to be fulfilled in it.

But the Lord commanded them what dispensation was going to be fulfilled in it. And the Lord commanded them not to weep for him, for it was not fitting to weep for him, but to hold back that mourning and weeping until the time.
And when that city fell into the hands of the enemies

who besieged it, and the beginning of what befell them was their calling blessed those who had not been born. And he recalled the woman who ate her own child, and how he said: "Blessed is the womb that has not given birth."
And now where is that kingdom, or the temple, or the walls and those high towers? Or where is that might of the Israelites?
Are they not all scattered to the ends of the earth, and through their worthlessness has not their kingdom too been laid waste?

And it seems to me that the Lord foretold that these things and things like them would happen, not for the sake of the force of the events to come. What benefit would the hearers have had from this, since these things were going to happen even against their will?

But they anticipated it by experience. Even though they did not do it with knowledge, they did it so that they would believe what is greater than it. For the testimony of this one, given by a deed, points to the truth of the other.
It is like a farmer telling someone who does not know the power of the field about it, and that person does not accept it on the strength of what the farmer says.

Then it is enough for the farmer if, with a single grain from one modius measure, he shows him the abundance of his words, so that when he comes to know the power of that one grain, he may know the power of all the seed that is in the modius.
For whoever sees a grain of wheat, or of barley, or of anything else, and knows
For after it fell into the furrow, it became a head [?].
And so it is with all of it. In the same way, the testimony of even one thing that has actually happened is enough for the resurrection.
And now the account of the resurrection is present among us in deed more than in word.

And how much greater the wonder of the resurrection is, and how hard to believe! For this reason the Lord began with small wonders, so that he might accustom our minds to the very great wonders. He did as a mother does when she nurtures a young infant,
and while its mouth is still tender and soft, she suckles it with milk,

and when its teeth begin to come in, she brings it bread that is warm and not hard, so that the bread's roughness does not hurt its palate, which is not used to it. Instead she chews it with her own mouth
until it is fit to be food suited to the strength of the one who eats it.
and then, at the completion of its strength, the child begins to eat dry food:
just so the Lord reared the weakness of the human soul with wonders and hedged it about with nurture, as if it were a small and immature child.
And first he began the foreshadowing of the resurrection with a sick person given up for lost. And that wonder was great,
yet it did not appear a wonder on this account, as with that great fever which was upon Peter's mother-in-law. And at once it vanished from her, after it had advanced and brought her near to death,
so that she rose and served all who were there.
And a little after this he added to the power in the case of the rich man's son, when the boy had been given up because of his sickness before the eyes of his people and had come near to death.
But his father cried out, called and begged him to hurry to come down while the boy had not yet died. And he raised up the boy who had come near to death.

And this was more astonishing, for he was far from that place, and from there he sent life to him by the richness of his authority. And again there follows upon it a higher wonder, which showed his going to the daughter of the ruler, and he delayed of his own will in going to her,
so that the healing which had been hidden might be revealed, that of the woman with the flow [?] of blood, and so that the death of the sick girl might [?] be completed.
And when the soul had departed from the body, and the time had come for beating the breast, for mourning and weeping over her death,
he gave a command to the girl, and she came alive at his command, as someone rises from sleep.
And in all this he was leading the weakness of the human race along a higher path and signifying it to them. And after this he rose higher, with a wonder and a greater deed,

so as to make faith in the resurrection easy for people. And again, Scripture tells us of a city in the land of Judah called Nain, in which there was a boy, the son of a widowed woman, and this boy had reached the full age of manhood, for Scripture calls him a young man.

And the writing tells us much in few words, while the narrative indicates abundant grief and mourning. For the mother of the dead man was a widow. And now do you not see how the book has indicated that great calamity in brief, and what its force is?

For that woman no longer had hope of bearing another son and being consoled from that grief, for the woman was a widow and she looked to no one else, and he was her only-begotten. For this reason her calamity was great and evident to all who are not strangers to nature.
And nowhere had that woman given birth to another apart from that child, and to him alone had she given milk to suck.
And he was the lamp of her table and her delight.
And he was the adornment of the streets in every way; in appearance he was full of charm, for his mother had him alone.
And for this reason they tried to hold the Lord back from going out to Galilee, for the Judeans held power at that time.
And the disciples were led away by the Lord, so that they might understand the beginning of the complete resurrection at Bethany.
And after four days from the death of Lazarus and the completion of everything
that is due to a dead person, both the wrapping in a shroud and the laying in the tomb, and that flesh had reached corruption and dissolution.
And they decayed in the earth, and the flesh was dissolved.
And that deed was great, at the time of the forcible dissolution of nature.
Then the matter of the rising of all, which was not yet believed, became clear and evident, for he did not now raise him from a severe illness, nor did he raise one who had been given over to death,
nor again does a little girl who has died rise, nor one like that young man who was being carried to the tomb and rose, set free,
but a man who lay dead in the tomb, dissolved and decayed,
to the point that even his own people would not allow the Lord to approach the tomb because of the stench that was in the tomb.

And this man by a single voice was brought to life and lived, and the report of the resurrection of the dead became true. And this is the fitting thing expected by all, which we have seen in this one man.
And just as it is to be at that resurrection of all, according to the word of the Apostle:
"The Lord will descend with a command and with the voice of the archangel and with lightning, and he will raise the dead to incorruption," so also now by a command,

by a voice, the one who had been given to the tomb thus drove death away as if it were sleep, and shook off the corruption that had fallen upon him from death. Whole and sound he rose up from the tomb, and the binding of his hands and feet could not prevent him from coming out.
And now does this seem little to you as proof of the resurrection of the dead, or do you still need yet another testimony for it?
But it seems to me that now the word was spoken in vain in Capernaum from the mouth of the Lord to the people, when he said, "Surely you will say this proverb to me:
"Physician, heal yourself."

But since the wonder of the resurrection of the dead had been confirmed in the bodies of others, it was even more fitting [?] that he confirm it in the flesh of his own humanity. And now you have seen the resurrection of the dead confirmed in others:

the girl who had come to the point of death, and the young man who had been deprived of life, and the child lying on the bier, and the decaying dead man who stank. All of these were brought back to life by a single word. But perhaps you still have doubts about those who died by the sword and by wounds, and wonder whether that grace and power might fall short in them? O Lord,
Look at him whose hands they nailed! Look at him whose side they pierced with a lance!
Put your fingers into the place of the nails! Put your hand into the wound of the spear, and feel how wide the wound is that your hand goes into!
For the spear had made a wide wound in the side.
And now, then, this one has risen from the dead, according to the word of the Apostle: "How do some say that there is no resurrection of the dead?"
And now, since all the things that previously came from the Lord by his command have been confirmed, to which the accomplished deeds bear witness, and we have come to know this not from words alone,
but by deeds, in those whom he brought back from death to life, what excuse is now left for those

who do not accept the resurrection of the dead and who wish, by that perishable wisdom of theirs, to conceal the truth? But we have learned from the prophet of the grace of the resurrection of the dead, as he said:
"You take their spirit from them, they fail and return to their earth;
and then you send forth your spirit, you create them, and you renew the face of the earth"; when he says:
"Then may the Lord rejoice in his creatures," when "sinners perish from the earth,"
for no one can be called a sinner where there is no sin. May the Lord will that we too have a share with them; for his is the authority and the might from age to age, Amen.

Chapter 26. And he said in chapter 26 that the resurrection is not [?]. For we find some people of weak understanding who measure their own power against the might of the Godhead, and they think that what is hard for us is hard for God too.
And they bring up the dead of long ago, the decay and corruption of their bodies, and those whom fire has consumed.
And they bring up as well flesh-eating beasts, and the case when a fish eats a man in the deep, and it then becomes food and nourishment for people, and from then on becomes a part of their flesh.
And they bring forward these and similar examples, which are not fit to be mentioned alongside the power of the Godhead and the glorious might of his authority.

By this they wish to overturn the doctrine of the resurrection: "For it is not possible," they say, "that God should rebuild every member of a person, which he had as his own, each one in its own place, just as they were."
First, then, let us with a few words refute the empty talkativeness of those

who suppose that their argument is credible. We, however, say and confess that bodies are to be dissolved and are to go back to that from which their constitution came, and that what is of the earth returns to the earth, as Scripture has said.
and air and water are joined to what is like them,

even if it has been eaten by beasts or by fish, and that human flesh has been mixed with their flesh, and has afterward become earth, or ash from fire, and all such things as they have mentioned: all of these are scattered within this world and not outside the world, but are joined to this same world.
But the divine Scripture says that this world is wholly established in the palm of the eye [?].
And now, if you know what you hold in your fist, how can you think that the power of God is weaker than your power, and that he would not perceive what he holds in the palm of his Godhead?

Chapter 27. And he said in the twenty-seventh chapter that it is possible for human bodies to be restored again from the four elements of the earth after their dissolution, and for those of one kind to be separated out, each in its own part, from all things. Perhaps you may suppose,

when you see the elements of this world, that it is somehow a difficult thing for the air that was air in us to return again, and the heat as heat, and the moisture as moisture, and likewise all the earth, each from its own kin, until what is its own returns to its own place from what is akin to it.
And do not be troubled about this form and this matter that you see among people, for this is beyond [?] the limits set for the mighty [?] by God.

I have seen at a human dwelling a flock of sheep, or of other animals, that many shepherds had gathered together. But when it is time to separate out each flock of the different kinds of those beasts, then they easily separate them, following their own custom and the marks stamped on them.
which are on them; each one of them retains its own distinctive property.
And if you picture this for yourself, you will not stray from the truth,

For the soul has an inclination, an attraction and a kinship toward the body in which it used to be. And that fine union was natural, because the soul ruled and dwelt in them, and from those natural marks,
in which what properly belongs to it is set apart, it recognizes it and gives it back.
And now, since the soul is drawn by the body again, with all its property and kinship, is there then any constraint upon that divine power [?] on this account?

For nothing has prevented it from being united with its kinship and its own property by that ineffable attraction. And it is indicated, for assurance concerning the soul, that marks and bodily traces exist there after its separation from bodily things, by those souls who are in hell, whose bodies have remained in the graves;
in whom there are bodily marks and signs remaining minutely within those souls, by which Lazarus is recognized, and the rich man also did not become unknown.
Therefore it is right for us to be convinced that the property of the body, which has remained, will at some time be separated out from what is akin to it, and all the more so for those
who minutely examine the matter of natures, for it is not wholly perishable and impossible to hold firm, but some part of it stands fast in us and some part is changed in its course,
for the body is changed in growth and diminution,

And a person changes his garment to suit his growth, the increase and decrease of his stature; for it is always with him unchanged, and in every change of the flesh by which the nature is recognized, there are recognizable marks that remain.

But the diseases that befall us we do not mean, nor is this discourse of ours about them, such as happen from suffering or from the causes of illness, which, when they come upon the body, become like a foreign face over the natural one,

and joined by this, the stable becomes united with the stable and remains in the divine soul, not by that part which flows and is changeable, but by the everlasting part which always stands firm in its own order.
For all the differences that exist among the races were altered by the qualities of nature in the blending.

And the mixture is nothing other than a combination of the elements. The elements are the root of everything that has been created, and from them the human body was created. Of necessity this body became a temple and dwelling of the soul, and that dwelling is not unknown to the one who dwells in it,
but at the time of the renewal it will draw that soul back to itself,
which was indisputably like its nature in those kinds.

And likewise this world must undergo dissolution from its proper states and a separation of its materials. It is like quicksilver: when it is poured out in a place where there is much rubbish and dust, it scatters and divides into many tiny parts and joins with nothing else,
and then what was scattered gathers again and unites with itself,

and nothing else joins with it, nor is anything of it lost. In this way, I think, will be the reuniting of human nature by the will of God, and what has been divided into many parts will at once be blended together, easily, without labor or mishap, for the nature of the Creator.

And the witness of this is the vision of the prophet Ezekiel. It is as when the earth easily makes plants sprout, without labor or hardship, not by force, whether wheat or any other seed, which cannot serve us as green or dry produce for use as food. And it changes at the time of growth, as it rises from the earth, some firm in its stance and some hollow, and that sprouted food is of many colors, having sprung up from the dryness of the earth and the moisture of water.
And then each one takes the form of its own nature and is differentiated in many forms and many colors.
Now if each of the plants is nourished from moisture and earth, and each of them is able to draw these and bring them into its own nature for growth and fruitfulness,
then what is astonishing in our statement about the resurrection of all people, since its manner is like the manner of the seeds of plants, which are drawn from their own natures?

For on every side we have true instruction about the resurrection, and it is not outside the knowledge gained by experience, which has been made known to us and confirmed among us, which was spoken of before and which we passed over in mentioning for the sake of the explanation of our natures. Now let us return again to that same explanation [?] and say
what is the cause of the beginning of this nature of ours, or what is our origin?

Now who would not marvel at this work of nature and its process: what it is that the womb receives, what its work is, and how it proceeds? Or do you not know that it is something diffuse and uniform throughout, which the womb holds bound within its depths, namely the seed, the beginning of our bodies? But once it is completed, formed within the womb like curd, shaped in outline and completed in structure,

who could distinguish it by understanding, or who could put it into words? Who could undertake to know that united nature and understand what follows from it: that this mean, contemptible thing, unsightly to look at and slight in power, is the beginning of that glorious and beautiful work, the completed body? And again, this work is great not only because of what follows, I mean the body. Rather, it is even more fitting to marvel at its beginning, at the work of the soul, and at the inquiry into these things.

Chapter 28. And he spoke in chapter 28 concerning those who say that souls were created before bodies, or else that bodies were created before souls, and the refutation of the argument of those who assert that souls dwell in many bodies. And it is not outside the knowledge gained by examination,

that which is discussed in the assemblies concerning the soul and the body. For some who came before us, at the outset of their discourses, supposed that souls are gathered together in a separate state of their own, and were created on that basis.
And indeed they are supposed to be subject to good and evil.

And as long as the soul remains in the good, it is far from mixture with the body. But when it falls away from that good, it inclines to the matter of the body, and betakes itself to such a dwelling, and again to others.

When they heard that word of the prophet Moses about the creation of man, they said that the body is prior to the soul in time, for God first took earth from the ground and made it into a man, and only afterward breathed into it a living soul.
And for this reason they gave the body priority over the soul, on the ground of its having been created first.
For they say that the soul was created for the sake of the body, so that the body would not be motionless, without breath and soul.
And everything that is created for the sake of something else is lesser in honor, as the holy Gospel says: "The soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing."

For these were created for their sake, since the existence of these made them [?]. But since these two arguments contend with one another and are open to doubt, and it is not yet clear which of them is true, I mean
those who said that souls exist alone, set apart, in activity, and again those who supposed that bodies came before souls,
it is now fitting for us to leave nothing between those two disputed positions without inquiry and clarification, through careful examination and full explanation.
This would require a long time and many words. But we will speak about it briefly, as far as we are able, and then begin on what we ourselves have observed,
in which the truth lies. Now those who put forward the first argument, which maintains that souls are prior to bodies,

Those who speak of successive times are not far removed in their teaching from those who say that souls migrate through many bodies. And if anyone anywhere should examine closely the arguments between these two disputes, he will find their teaching turned aside from the truth, for one of the teachers said
that a certain man put on the body of a woman, and flew up with the birds, and sprouted with the meadows, and came to be in the life of fish.
And I think that in this statement of his he has fittingly told us something that matches his own foolishness.
For this talk resembles the chatter of frogs and jackdaws, the speechlessness of fish, and the senselessness of plants.
And the cause of this error for those who devise such things was the idea that souls are older than bodies.
But if the soul, which is spiritual, through its inclination toward the coarseness of evil, came to be in a body of flesh,
and the fleshly body is more prone to the passions than that spiritual, bodiless nature, then this compels the soul toward occasions of sin through its many migrations from body to body.

And it would be more bound to sin at the last than at the first, for the sickness of the human soul has been likened to the beasts, so that it would without doubt be close to the nature of beasts and to that migration from one beastly state to another.
Therefore it is indeed unceasing in this evil, for the ceasing of evil is the beginning of virtue, and virtue is not found among beasts.
So now the soul indeed always moves toward evil, through its constant migration to a nature inferior

to the one in which it is. And just as the sensitive is inferior to the rational power, so too the power of those things that have no sensation is lesser than those that have sensation. And whoever teaches and interprets their doctrines would be migrating from one coarse state to another.

For the conclusion of their teaching points to the complete corruption of the soul, since the soul that departs from its proper order and becomes suited to evil does not stop, but changes from place to place.
And its end is decay from rationality into beastliness, and from beastliness it would arrive at the loss of sensation.
And it would draw near to those insensible, soulless plants, and after that not even existence would be found among them.
And as they philosophize on that point, they would harm the soul, where it has no road onward, for it has no means of returning to the honor of its own good.

And now their teaching implies that life in plants is higher than life in the human body, and their teaching has made it plain that the soul in its course sinks downward in sorrow until it reaches dissolution.

And now, according to their teaching, without doubt either the soul would perish in burning along with the plants, or they would bring it back again to human life from the life of plants, or they would declare that plant life is better than that spiritual life from which it has fallen.

And from there it would go back again to that better state. And so the teaching of those who say that souls existed before bodies, and that souls came to be in bodies through their inclination to evil, is unstable and unproven.

As for those who say that the soul was created after the body, our argument refutes their claims by means of those earlier arguments of ours. Their statements are refuted and unacceptable in every respect.
But the true and trustworthy account, which stands between those two positions and opposes them, is the one we state:

that the soul did not pass into the body because of its heaviness and downward inclination, nor again do we say that the soul was created after the body, but that man was created all at once, by nature.

Chapter 29. And in the twenty-ninth chapter he set out an inquiry which shows that the essence of soul and body is united. And again, let no one suppose from our words that man was first created in the form of an idol, and that the creation of the soul was therefore added to him. For if this were so, would the nature of clay then be superior to the rational nature?
But in fact man is one by nature, consisting of soul and body, and the beginning of their formation is one,
so that man should not be prior to himself and higher than himself, since the body of plants is earlier than what has a soul.
But we say again, as we said before, that God by his power created man entirely complete, as the book testifies,
that "God knows all things before their creation." And when he created,

he did not place one of the parts before another: he did not put the soul before the body, nor the body before the soul, lest man should be set against his own soul, whether by that property or by a separation of times. But since our created being is twofold, outward and inward,

if one is prior to the other, then surely the power of the Creator was not complete in it, for it would have remained without completeness and would have divided their labor by a distribution of the work.
And just as in a grain of wheat, or in other seeds, there is the power of bringing itself forth, which is seen in stalks and joints, in leaves and in bearded seed, and no one would say
that within the boundary of its own nature one part has any priority over another, but rather it appears in its own order, and this appearing of it takes place along the path of its own nature,

so likewise we say concerning the propagation of human beings, that at the beginning of its formation the nature was present in potency, and its manifestation came in fullness according to its own order. It is not that it needed anything outside its own nature for its completion,
for the soul did not exist without the body, nor the body without the soul,
but the beginning of both is one, first by the command and will of God, and afterward by the bringing forth of birth,

for in human propagation it cannot be conceived that one thing was in any way before or after another in the bodily sowing. Likewise, in the property of the soul it is not possible either that one should be before or after another in operation,
for it is not that some other power was joined to the body, which was divided among the members and joints.

but it was moving according to its own order in the natural process. In the same way we ought to understand about the soul that, although in its activity it is invisible at the beginning of motion, it undoubtedly dwells in its own body. So too we say of the infant coming out of the womb
that the soul is present in it in potential, though not fully. It remains invisible until it is brought to completion in activity, together with the completion of the body's nature.
For the power of seeding in it, which goes forth, does not come from dead flesh devoid of soul,
but from the life of the soul.

Therefore it is fitting for us, as I think, to say that this flesh is not dead, without soul, since it comes forth from a living being, because of the cause of its life. For whatever is in a soulless body is dead without doubt. And death is nothing other than the privation of soul, for what is lacking does not come before what exists.

But if the soulless, which is the death of the soul, is prior to the soul, [?], then let privation not be before possession, for this statement is false. But if someone wishes to know, by way of demonstration,
that this part is living,
he is able to learn it from the distinct acts that separate the living from the dead,
for speech, action and movement make known the life of a human being.
But what is frozen and motionless is nothing other than dead.

When we have looked at that flesh, stripped of hair and bones and limbs, let us not say that there is one nature and another, the one prior to the other; rather, these things are present in it in potency,
although they are invisible and unmanifest in it. We speak in the same way about the spiritual part: for although there is as yet no speech in it at all, nor yet desire and glory, nor anything else

that is seen in the soul, yet we know that it abides in it by nature. Rather, it comes forth at the time of its own completion, together with the completion of the body and the growth of its activity.
And just as, when a human being has been completed in form, the activity of the soul comes to be in complete deeds,
so also, while he is in his beginning, there is from time to time whatever need of activity he requires, in the mind of infancy, which is its dwelling.
And it cannot be said that anyone has encountered the soul except in its own house. And just as clay cannot take on an engraving except from the seal with which the kneaded clay is stamped,

And just as the body comes from mean and contemptible earth to that great glory, so too the activity of the soul corresponds to the measure in which its own vessel, its dwelling place, can receive it. In this way it extends, expands, and grows,
for the conception is like a root, whose power of growth and nourishment lay hidden within the earth. With its small capacity it cannot contain what is greater than itself.
But when the shoot of that root sprouts up and passes through the face of the earth and receives the air of the sun, then the grace of sensation shines forth upon it and adorns it.

And it reaches full growth and the measure of fruitfulness, and there shines within it the likeness of the power of reason. These things do not appear immediately and all at once. Rather, as the vessel reaches completeness and size, and in step with its advance [?], it becomes fruitful according to the power that is present in it.

But if you want to know what the power of the soul is within the structure of the body, then look at yourself, as Moses says, so that you may understand the work of the soul as if you were reading it from a book. In this way you will understand it better than through any spoken word, from its many works in the body and in all its parts.
And I think that investigating this with words is superfluous, like someone describing distant things and the boundaries of the earth and its inhabited regions.
Now let someone examine himself: would he still need a teacher and informant about his own nature? Let a person see the cause of his own life,

or from where this flesh comes to be fitted, for he will learn what the soul is occupied with at the first beginning of its creation, so that he may believe that this flesh was not first created dead and without soul.
Nor does seed fall into a dead and soulless place, just as plants or grains are not sown in salty and barren ground.

For the ground that receives the seed or the plants does not have living power, as though it were giving this from outside. And if this were so, then withered trees would be found to receive such power from the ground,
but there is within it a life hidden in its own proper power, by which it draws in the soil of the earth and sucks it up, and by this it puts forth roots and bark and branches,
until the plant is brought to completion by the power of nature that is within it, and from it comes the nourishment proper to trees, or plants, or greens.
Chapter 30. And in the thirtieth chapter he set out a discourse drawn from the physicians, which teaches about the members of human bodies in their creation.

And that discourse is a compilation. Now, concerning the creation of our bodies, anyone can understand by true investigation, through the power that he is taught by his own nature, through knowledge and life, and through sensation. For the nature of every person is its own teacher,
but it is possible for us to make plain what the wise have traced out in detail in books concerning the knowledge of it,

by which some people came to know the position of all the members within us, when they investigated it by laying bodies open and by opening wounds. And some understood the purpose for which each member of the body was created.
And this became, for those who labor at it, an informant by way of explanation, in which there is complete understanding.
But if anyone wishes to receive this teaching from the Church, so as to have no need of anything from those outside,

for thus it is fitting for those spiritual flocks, according to the word of the Savior, that: "They shall not hear the voice of a stranger." But now let us turn to the discourse and speak according to our ability.
We see these three things in the nature of our bodies, for the sake of which all our members were created:

some for life, and some for the richness of life, and some for the continuance of birth and the securing of the race. But as for the members within us that follow upon these, the life of a human being cannot come about from them, but we see it in those three:
the head, the heart and the liver.
And the increase of nature in good things comes about from the richness of life that was granted to man, which is a vessel,
in which the sense organs are located, for these cannot give us life,
since our life is possible even without them, although without them our life is not one of enjoyment.

And the third is this, from which comes the continuance of offspring and the securing of the lineage. There are also other parts in the body that share with these in supplementing and benefiting them,
such as the stomach and the lung. For it is the lung that rouses [?] the fire of the heart, and the stomach receives food into its own vessels.
Now, since the constitution of our nature is divided among these parts, it appears [?] that the vital power in us does not rest on one single part alone,
but nature has distributed its causes among the individual members, and each of them is compelled to assist the others.

But what is required for the safeguarding of life and the adornment of nature is manifold and varied in its divisions. Yet I wish first to set out briefly that in which the maintenance of our life consists.
The material of the body is entirely common to all the members. And for now let us pass over that discussion, for a discourse on nature is of no use to us at present for a brief investigation.
For it is evident to all that these elements of this world are found in our nature;
I mean the portion of heat and cold, of moisture and dryness.
And we see that there are three powers that govern life: one of them warms the body with its heat, and the second power moistens the heat,

so that its mixture may be balanced, and so that the moisture may not perish through the intensity of the heat, and again so that the heat may not be quenched by an excess of moisture. And the third power gathers together what is scattered, by the joining of the sinews,
which are connected to all the members by the self-moving power; and whenever the power fails, that member becomes dead and deprived of the self-moving spirit.
And first we should examine carefully the creation of our bodily nature. Why is this member hard and insensible, not receptive of the sensing nature, namely the bones within us,
just like the plants of the earth, which have some share of life, since they grow and are nourished, and yet the insensibility in them does not receive sensation?
For this reason there must be in it a power of softness, receptive of an impression, as when wax receives the imprint from a seal,
for it has a balanced mixture of moist and dry, since what is too moist does not receive the imprint of the seal, and neither, again, does hardness receive it in like manner.
And this was so that living creatures should lack [?] the most honorable sense, we mean touch.

And because soft bodies, lacking dryness, are without extension and immobile, like a sea sponge, which is fattened and grows greatly in the sea from moisture and does not move, for this reason these hard, dry bones were mixed in and were anointed with the moisture of the flesh. They became joined and articulated with one another and fashioned together with sinews, and because of this the body was united and completed and stood upright and strong.
And those dry, hard bones became bearers of the flesh, which is heavy with moisture.
And in it the bones are not removed and separated from the flesh.
If man were immobile, standing in one place like the trees, and did not go about on feet or work with his hands to support his life,
For this reason man is a vessel self-moved by the spirit, master of his own will, fashioned together from many sinews.
Because of this the skills of the hands came into being, and his many kinds of service, beautiful in all the arts.

And because of it came about the movement of the hand and the turning of the head, the action of the jaws, the closing and opening of the eyes, and the other movements of the ligaments by means of the sinews,
which contract and extend; and that moving power has its motion from the course of the spirit, by the voluntary governance of all the members.

But the root of the movement of the sinews is the whole membrane of the head. From this point on we no longer need an inquiry concerning the living members, since the movement of their operations is evident.
And what informs us that the brain is the cause of life is this fact,
This becomes evident from what it suffers: for when some wound strikes the membrane of the brain, death comes swiftly, and the person no longer survives that wound.
The brain is like a foundation on which a tower is built. When the foundation gives way, the upper part also collapses, for truly the brain is the giver of life.
And again we see that in everything that is removed from life, its condition turns to cold and heat departs from it.
By this, again, we know that heat too is a cause of life, for whatever lacks it becomes dead, and by its presence the life of living beings exists.
But the beginning and root of this is the heart, from which many tubes come out, and through them the living spirit is mixed into every path with fiery heat.
For heat needs natural nourishment for its subsistence, for fire cannot stand by itself,

But by its entry into it, through which it is nourished — for this reason streams of blood go out from the liver, like breath from [?], apart from water [?], gathered together with warm breaths toward the whole body, so that the two may not be separated and life perish.
For when one increases over the other, it destroys life.

But rich, and in need of nothing, is no one but God alone. Man, on account of his feebleness and helplessness, needs causes that sustain his nature. For this reason also those three powers which we mentioned, because of which the body stands, need matter to take in for their subsistence and firmness.
And that fountain of blood,

which is the liver, is a material that nourishes by means of foods and drinks. It is like snow lying on the summits of mountains: its moisture raises up and multiplies the springs of water in the ravines of the mountains. That moisture is squeezed and pressed from its depth until it comes out through channels, and springs of water rise up.
But the breath that is in the heart receives its nourishment from the member that is its brother, namely the lung, which is a vessel that brings in air through that pipe
which it joins from the mouth, and through which it draws in breath from the air outside.
And in the midst of it is the heart, having the nature of that fire which is ever in motion.

And as with the bellows of smiths, it gathers a fine breeze from the nearby air, fills its vessel, and cools the heat of that fire-like thing. And then it passes it to the pulsing channels of the heart.
This it does without ceasing, taking some in from outside by drawing it in, and driving some out from within by expelling it.
But I think that this is the cause of the sighing that comes upon a person, [?] is from [?] kind.
