But when the mind is [?] from something, or when it rests at the time of sleep for the repose of the body, breathing still does not cease, even though the will does not accompany it.
And I think, concerning the heart, since it is enclosed by the lung on the rear side, that its contraction and expansion are the cause of the movement of the lung.
For this reason the lung is built thin, like a sponge, with many channels, and fused together with the [?]; and when it draws together and is pressed in,
it is narrowed, and the breath within it bursts out through the mouth; but when it opens and expands, it draws in breath from the air by suction.

And this is the reason why a person breathes, by that twofold fire-like [?] ever remaining; for the property of heat is the motion of activity, and we see its beginning in the heart, and through the persistence of motion this member, which through the lung's taking in of air, [?] that air remaining with it always.

And for this reason, when that heat increases beyond measure, the breathing becomes rapid, continuous, high and broken, at the time of fever and of other illnesses too, until nature strives to quench that flame of heat by taking in air anew, again and again.
And because our nature is poor, and it needs many causes for its subsistence,
not only the air that cools the heat from outside, in the manner of the subsistence of animals, but it also needs nourishment that sustains and replenishes.
And for this reason, by food and drink that deficiency which is in our bodies is made up, from the power that brings them in.

And there is help for this heat that is in the body through the working of nature. For the highest and chief of the members is the heart, which, as we said, conveys that heat of breath and life to all the members. The Creator created it so that it would hold the whole body by its powers.
And this is so that nothing of his arrangement should remain idle and useless. For this reason the place of the heart was made behind the lung.
And when its movement stops, the lung draws it in and expands to receive the air, and it constricts the outgoing pipes in the organ of breathing, to expel the remainder left over from it.
And the place of the stomach is close by, in front of the heart, so that the heart may warm it,
so that it may function well in its own work and in the digestion of foods,
for the channel of foods and the channel of breath are close to one another, joined to each other side by side along their length.
And the descent of both of them is at first by a single path. But when it reaches the inner depth, toward the moisture
that is in the liver, it leaves to that moisture the property of fiery heat, which resembles the color of blood.
And from the liver come forth two outlets, resembling channels, in which are breath and blood,
so that the blood may be a stream, going by the aid of the heat and spreading through the whole body, and through all the vessels it is divided and scattered into all the limbs.
And this happens by the union of the two powers
that are life-giving and principal: I mean the heat, which conveys to the moisture the governance of the power of life, which is the membrane of the head,
from which comes the movement of all the sinews, and the contraction and extension of the cords,
which moves all the members of the body. And through this they are nourished and grow, by the union of the two fine powers, which is the brain [?].

And by its nourishment the membrane that clothes the brain is nourished in turn. And this membrane is a substance that feeds from above down to below, containing the many parts that are the vertebrae of the spine. And that nourishment in turn feeds also the marrows that are in all the bones; it is divided among the sinews and cords, and each goes its own way. And when it goes down into the stomach, it does not rest until it melts it with its heat, like a furnace, and sends it to the passages that follow, and the coarse is separated from the fine. The fine reaches the liver through its own channels, while the coarse goes out into the wide places of the intestine. And the food stays in its place for some time, so that it may not leave quickly and a person need food without pause, and on account of it have no leisure, like the beasts. And help is needed from the liver through the action of heat, so that it may change the moist matter that comes to it and make it into blood.

But the place of the liver is far from the heart, for it was not fitting that that principal member, which is the root of the power of life, should be crushed by another, or that the mind of the heat should be destroyed by the descending cord-like passage, which is called the gullet. For this reason a passage was made from the heart to the liver, which conveys the fiery breath, and this is the governor of all movements and goings. For this reason it was fitting that they should have as a covering the breastplate, which is constructed of bones and many sinews.
And within it it is firmly kept and guarded, as a king dwells within an inner curtain.
And in the same way we see the heart, for it is enclosed as in a house,
made firm by the enclosure of the ribs around it, and from behind it is strengthened by the bones of the spine, walled in on both sides.
On the front side the chest and the yoke-bones are spread over it as a covering against injuries.
And as you have seen with those who work the land, when they distribute channels of water in order to moisten the ground,

but let us also compare it to a garden, in which there are trees of many colors and plants of various kinds, differing in color and form and taste, and each one grows with its own particular property from one water.
And the moistening power of them all is one by nature, while the particular property of those that receive the nourishment is divided in many ways, in diverse conditions.
And it becomes bitterness in the tree of the [?] and deadly in the tree of the [?], whose nut is a deadly poison. And its power is one thing in saffron, another in balsam, and another in a plant:
in some it is cold, in some hot, and in some the power is in a moderate state.
And the lily and the rose have a sweet fragrance, and the fig and the pear have sweetness, and the vine brings forth the grape, and from it comes the power of wine.
And the other things too, which spring up from one earth and from one moisture, come forth and grow in many kinds, varied in their qualities.
And we see this pattern in our own garden, from spiritual nature, and still more from the Lord of nature.

bones and cartilages and veins and cords and sinews and flesh and fat and hair and nails, and eyes that see many colors and ears that hear various sounds, which is suited to these by distinct properties,
remote from one another, from one nourishment, which is changed in each of the members according to their particular property.
For what reaches the eye is blended with that seeing member and with the [?] membranes of the pupils.

And what reaches the organ of hearing is blended into the nature of hearing; and in the lips the nourishment spreads out, in the bones it hardens and becomes solid, and in the marrow it softens and grows tender; and for the growth of hair, by that separating vapor, if it goes out through round channels,
the hair becomes curly, and if it goes out straight, the hair is [?] and reed-like.
But we have strayed from the inquiry into the matter we were engaged in, the natural one, which is deep.
And that was when we were inquiring how or from what each member was established for life, and for the abundance of life, and also for the things that follow these, as we divided them at first.
For the thought for which the inquiry was made had become evident, and we had come to know
that the root of our constitution is neither soul without body nor body without soul, but it comes to be from living, ensouled bodies by that first birth,

For nature is [?] and receptive, of those things that cause its own growth, and it appears first in all its members. For the soul is to be understood as being in this structure through the power brought to completion that is present in this vessel,
and in that completion it appears and is revealed, as can be seen in the work of stone-carvers. For when the carver wishes to make a statue,

first cuts a block out of the mountain, and then shapes it into a form not unrecognizable to those who see it, and then prepares it by adding to the work, until it reaches the perfection of the form he wishes,
But the material of the stone had not attained the form,
rather, the form was what would change [?] the material. In the same way, understand this concerning the soul,

for the Nature that is creator of all things took from the human material and made it into a statue, just as a sculptor gradually, over time, brings the form to completion in the material, from the beginning to the end.
so too the carving of the soul of our nature is incomplete at its first beginning, and complete at its completion.

And at some point it would have been complete, if the onset of evil had not cut it off from that perfect grace. The created state became deficient, when otherwise the image of God would have shone forth within it.
And the soul of man came to travel toward that same perfection by labor and journeying.
The glorious apostle Paul writes of this to the Corinthians and says: "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, but when I became a man, I left behind the things of childhood."
For the soul of a child is not one soul and that of a man another; rather, it is incomplete in the child and complete in the man.
And just as we say of growing plants that they are nevertheless alive, for whatever has a share of life and motion is not called soulless, nor incomplete, when it has life.

For when a plant has come into being, it is also growing, but it has not reached the activity of sense-perception. So too in beasts there is a beastly, perceiving soul, and it has not reached perfection, which is the gift of speech and understanding.

For this reason we say that the true, perfected soul is the human one, recognizable from all its activities. But whatever is outside of it is called a soul by name only and not truly, since it is incomplete.
But there is in it an active, [?] part, as we have heard from Moses about the creation of man, that it is in man through his inclination toward evil,
concerning which the Apostle also teaches and says:
"Strip off the old man and put on the new man, renewed in the likeness of his Creator."
But may it be granted to us to attain once more that grace of the likeness of God with which God created man in the beginning, when he said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness,"
to whom belong glory and power, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
